- **Subagent dispatch mechanism — stateless per-turn invocation across harnesses (Antigravity `invoke_subagent` vs Claude Code `Task`) (2026-10-01)**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTYF5W48001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Trajectory and architectural analysis establishing that subagent turns must always be dispatched as fresh, stateless invocations rather than stateful conversational continuations:
  
  - **Incident — Grapher Turn 2 transcript bloat (220 steps, 278 KB)**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTYF5W48002' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> In Turn 2 of `### promote-and-fix-subagent-tool-gap`, Orchestrator dispatched Grapher via `send_message` targeting its Turn 1 conversation ID (`97ddc9af`). This appended Turn 2 into Turn 1's history rather than resetting context. By the end of Turn 2, Grapher's transcript reached 220 steps and ~278 KB, dragging along Turn 1's Apeiron service restart attempts, interactive prompt stalls, and 50-line JSON-LD grep dumps.
  - **Root cause — Antigravity built-in continuation heuristic vs Aperas memory model**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTYF5W48003' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Antigravity's generic harness prompt advises agents to send follow-up messages to existing subagents to "conserve resources" for natural continuations. This advice directly contradicts Aperas's core architectural principle: **The Apeiron graph and `.threads/{role}.md` are the working memory, not the LLM's conversation history.** Reusing subagents causes context rot, token bloat, and degrades multi-turn reasoning.
  - **Harness compatibility comparison — Claude Code `Task` vs Antigravity `invoke_subagent`**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTYF5W48004' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> In Claude Code, subagent delegation via the `Task` tool is inherently ephemeral and stateless: each `Task` invocation is a fresh instance with zero prior session history (Claude Code has no `send_message` equivalent). Antigravity supports both `invoke_subagent` (stateless fresh spawn) and `send_message` (stateful continuation). Mandating `invoke_subagent` per turn in Antigravity unifies behavior with Claude Code's native execution model.
  - **Orchestrator skill guidance & harness-agnostic wording**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTYF5W48005' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> `skills/aperas-orchestrator/SKILL.md` must explicitly mandate stateless per-turn dispatch using universal discipline paired with harness tool mappings:
    
    - *Universal rule*: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTYF5W48006' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Always dispatch a fresh subagent instance for every turn; subagents in Aperas are stateless workers. Never carry conversation history across turns.
    - *Tool mappings*: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTYF5W48007' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> In Antigravity, call `invoke_subagent` (never `send_message` across distinct turns); in Claude Code, call `Task`.
    - *Context restoration*: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTYF5W48008' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Every turn recovers state cleanly through the view (`aperas tree --view <p>-orchestrator-<role>`) and the thread (`.threads/<role>.md`).
- **Verification command scope — `npm run verify` is code-only (2026-10-01)**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTZJE8C8001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> `npm run verify` (even with `verify:slow` separated) is a heavy test suite reserved strictly for code/engine changes. It must never be executed during skill-only tasks. Skill-only verification relies solely on `python3 skills/aperas/scripts/skill_drift.py` and `npm run aperas -- check-links`. Running `verify` for skill edits causes unnecessary hangs, compute waste, and test timeouts.
- **Mistaking shadows for the source — root causes of `.threads/` disk access and elevating "node reference, not file path" to Philosophy #1 (2026-10-01)**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTZJGWW0001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Detailed analysis of why orchestrators and subagents repeatedly attempt to access `.threads/` using filesystem tools (`ls`, `cat`, `view_file`) in `Aperas/`:
  
  - **Root Cause 1 — The File Mirage (POSIX and Git vocabulary)**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTZQR3SG002' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> The notation `.threads/` (leading dot = hidden directory), `.md` extension, description as "Git-ignored" (which applies only to disk files), and phrasing like "creates in `.threads/grapher.md`" strongly trigger the LLM's filesystem schema rather than the graph-node schema.
  - **Root Cause 2 — The Step 1 CLI Tool Void**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTZQR3SR000' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Step 1 instructs Orchestrators to "create `## <topic>` and `### <task>` in `.threads/grapher.md`", but provides zero CLI recipes for resolving thread root IDs or inserting headings without file access. Lacking a graph recipe, agents fall back to `ls` and `cat`.
  - **Root Cause 3 — Two-repo CWD conflation**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTZQR3SR001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Terminal execution is anchored in `$CWD` (`Aperas/`), while graph artifacts are rooted in `AperasKG/artifacts/`. Agents mistakenly resolve relative thread paths against `$CWD`.
  - **Symptom & philosophical breach — violating Philosophy #1 ("No inspection of the shadows")**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTZQR3SR002' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Direct file access inspects projected shadows stripped of graph state, backlinks, and view hierarchy.
  - **Promoting "Node Reference, Not File Path" to Section 1 Philosophy**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTZQR3SR003' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> In v4, "An `artifacts/**.md` path in your hand is a node reference, not a file path" was placed in Section 2 as an operational gate. It must be elevated to a core bullet point in Section 1 Philosophy (*The Apeiron is the source*) to govern the entire skill.
  - **Structural resolution across discipline and CLI runbooks**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CTZQR3SR004' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>
    
    - Reject creating symlinks in `Aperas/` (which merely codifies and facilitates the bad reflex).
    - Provide explicit CLI recipes for Step 1 thread initialization (`aperas show .threads/grapher.md`, `aperas tree .threads/grapher.md`, piping heading inserts).
    - Enforce graph-first traversal via views (`aperas tree --view`) and CLI inspection (`aperas show`, `aperas unfold`).
- **Skill size audit — Claude Code 5,000-token compaction threshold and progressive disclosure refactor (2026-10-01)**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CV2ZRHWR001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Detailed analysis of base skill growth (497 lines, 30.6 KB, ~5,800 tokens) against harness thresholds, identifying compaction truncation in Claude Code and defining the progressive disclosure refactoring architecture:
  
  - **Current file metrics**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CV2ZRHWR002' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> `skills/aperas/SKILL.md` has expanded to 497 lines and 30,572 bytes (~5,500–6,000 tokens), sitting at 99.4% of the 500-line recommended ceiling and exceeding the 5,000-token budget.
  - **Compaction truncation risk in Claude Code**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CV2ZRHWR003' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> In Claude Code, skills are loaded into context upon trigger. When conversation context approaches limits, Claude Code executes context compaction. Skills that exceed the 5,000-token threshold are subject to aggressive truncation and summarization during compaction. This drops detailed CLI syntax rules, anchor constraints, and operational gates mid-session, causing subagents to make blind edits or read engine source code.
  - **Antigravity tool bounds vs. self-truncation**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CV2ZRHWR004' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Antigravity's `view_file` tool supports up to 800 lines and 46 KB, so `SKILL.md` fits in a single view call. However, subagents self-truncate reads (e.g. requesting lines 1–100 or 1–250). While the restored Table of Contents mitigates initial discovery, long files remain vulnerable to incomplete context loading.
  - **Refactoring architecture (Progressive Disclosure)**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CV2ZRHWR005' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>
    
    - Retain Section 1 Philosophy, Section 2 Orientation, Section 3 Discipline (roles, 9-step task loop, thread rules), and a concise command cheatsheet in a lean core `SKILL.md` (~250–300 lines, ~3,000 tokens).
    - Move Section 4's deep CLI syntax, AST piping rules, anchor placement, list item update subtleties, and troubleshooting into an on-demand reference document: `skills/aperas/references/mechanics.md`.
    - Subagents load the lean core skill by default, and only consult `references/mechanics.md` when executing non-trivial graph mutations.

### Grapher skill has no skill-record delta or version-bump protocol <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVK447WR001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

The `Supersedes:` convention, the rule that a removed unit needs a `Supersedes:`-only entry, and the checker's folding of a `---` under a bullet into that bullet's unit are not in the Grapher skill; the grapher worked them out by reading the drift checker's code and its output.

Still unwritten in any skill: who bumps a `Status:` line and when, with the skill edit or with the delta.

[Decision — the Status guard is a checker plus one line](#id/BlockNode:00CVKQEDTG001) put that into the Grapher skill's drift section as one sentence, and [`skill_drift.py` now fails](#id/BlockNode:00CVKV9DPG002) when the newest delta's version differs from the `Status:` lines. - **Finding — the service has dropped repeatedly during one task**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVK46RQ8001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> In the skill-edit task at least six commands failed because the service was unreachable: the orchestrator's `aperas project`, two of the orchestrator's `insert` calls (the coder's Turn 1 Ask and the grapher's Turn 3 Ask), one in the grapher's Turn 2, and two in the grapher's Turn 3 (an `update`, then a `project`, `tree` and `check-links` sequence). Earlier friction entry: [Friction — ApeironNgn service dropped between commands](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00CVJPV978001).
  
  - Promoted to [A command can fail with "No ApeironNgn service running" while the service is up, and an unchanged retry works](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVMPABY8001)

That pid had started at 15:42 local and was the one the commands had been using. - **Observation — a spurious "not running" while the service was up, again**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVKGEBNG000' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> In the `check-links` issue turn, the grapher's `aperas insert` and `aperas project` each failed twice with "No ApeironNgn service running" while the service was running, and an unchanged retry worked both times. This matches the earlier observation that the process stayed alive during a drop, and points at the client's discovery or connection step, not the service dying.

- **Observation — the service wedged for over 25 minutes during the grapher's prune, and was killed**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVNYDD18001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> While pruning finished thread tasks with `aperas remove`, the grapher saw the service freeze for 5.4 and about 12 minutes after removing tasks of 42 and 31 live blocks. It then ran `aperas service restart`, which never completed. The old process (pid 220722, about 3.4 hours up) climbed from 4.7 to 5.8 GB resident at roughly 40–50 MB a minute, ran two threads at 100% CPU, wrote nothing, and answered no command, while its lock file said "ready" and system memory was down to a few hundred MB free. Its own swapped memory was 26 MB, so it was not swapping. A normal stop (`aperas service stop`) failed after 10 s, and at the user's instruction ("Just stop it -- clearly stuck!") the process was killed with SIGKILL at 19:42 after copying the store directory to the scratchpad. A fresh service needed about 60 seconds to answer, was already at 1.5 GB after two minutes, and still dropped commands intermittently while it started.
- **Observation — what the kill lost and kept**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVNYDD18002' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Kept: every Freeflow entry and Ask recorded before about 19:00 and the Turn 5 Ask. Lost: the grapher's thread prune tombstones (six checked, all live again with no `tombstonedAt`), the grapher's stall-issue text, and the orchestrator's note on service memory (written again here). The thread store file still showed a write time of 18:26 although it held newer nodes, so what reached disk and when is not clear.
- **Observation — the service reports 323 duplicate ids on start**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVNYDD1G000' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> The start-up log says "323 duplicate @id(s) in the mirror — quads from every occurrence merged onto one subject, so at most one document per id survives the next dehydrate". A scan of every `.jsonld` file in the store found only two ids in more than one place (`BlockNode:00CR9MFS68001` and `BlockNode:00CRBH4RHR001`, in both the main and the thread store). The 323 is not explained.
- **Hypothesis — the stall is the same mechanism as the earlier process-lifetime slowdown**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVNYDD1G001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (user: "This sweep, I think, links to the issue of the very long run of `verify` which forced us to split it to `verify:slow`") The issue [verify slowdown](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CJ0202MG001) recorded a process-lifetime slowdown that only a fresh process reset (oxigraph's WASM footprint at about 1 GB and V8 heap size were ruled out), and [why isolation helps](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CJ0HX2Y0000) says to profile with `--prof` or `--trace-deopt` if it recurs where a process split is not viable. The service is a long-lived process where a split is not viable. Differences: the earlier slowdown was slower steps, not multi-minute stalls, and the footprint is now about 5 GB. Not tested. A test that separates the two causes: time one large `remove` on a fresh service and the same `remove` after a long uptime.

- **Observation — the monitor's two memory series, and what they say about the wedged service**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVP1M920001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (user, from the system memory monitor, twice: "the mem just dropped, check the service!", and later a screenshot) The monitor draws two series. The light-cyan "Active" memory dropped many times before the service was stopped and did not move at the kill; only the dark-cyan "Allocated" memory dropped at the kill. The orchestrator's first reading of the screenshot, that Active dropped once before and again at the kill, was wrong. The orchestrator's samples of the service's resident size rose the whole time (4.74 GB at 19:20, 5.01 at 19:26, 5.66 at 19:40, 5.76 at 19:42, just before the stop), with a gap in sampling between 19:28 and 19:40, and after the kill available memory rose from 3.3 GB to 7.9 GB, the freed 5.8 GB less the fresh service's 1.1 GB. Reading: because Active did not fall when the 5.8 GB service was killed, its memory was not in Active, which counts pages recently touched. So the service held about 5.8 GB it was not touching while its CPU stayed at 100% on two threads: a loop on a small working set, not work across the whole heap, which weakens the garbage-collection explanation. The repeated drops in Active before the kill were then something else, with the short-lived `aperas` client processes (each command starts its own node process) the obvious candidate; not tested. Both readings are untested.
- **Open — a sampler for the next stall**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVP1M928000' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> Log every 10 seconds, for the service pid: resident size, Active and Inactive anon pages (`smaps_rollup`), per-thread CPU and state, and the system's available memory, to a file, so a drop can be matched to a time afterwards.

All five subagent runs (grapher Turns 1–3, coder Turns 1–2) ended with a one-line plain message (82 chars at most) and put a full report of 11–37 lines into the hand-back. It resolves four roots today (the v4 snapshot and the v4.1, v4.2 and v4.3 deltas). The guard fits in `main()` at `:212-214`, after `roots = recorded_roots(blocks)` and the "no snapshot or delta sections found" exit; the newest delta is the last delta entry of `roots` (or the snapshot when there is none), and `skills = find_skill_files()` at `:210` already holds the four files (`aperas/SKILL.md` plus `sorted(glob("aperas-*/SKILL.md"))`, `:56-65`), which exclude `kg-doc-ingest`, so a guard over `skills` is automatically the four-file set while a repo-wide `Status:` search would fail on `kg-doc-ingest`'s `v0`. Versions compare as tuples after trimming trailing zeros, so `(4,)` equals `(4, 0)`. The comparison is independent of `--added` and `--dropped`: the printing blocks are gated by `both or args.added` (`:228`) and `both or args.dropped` (`:241`), so where it runs is a design choice. Constraints the guard must respect: the "superseded, accounted for" list (`accounted`, `:248`) is 170 lines on every run and is not a finding, so it must stay out of the exit status; the header docstring (`:14`, `:25-30`) and the `--added` and `--dropped` help text would need to state the exit rule. Existing open issues on the same checker that the edit does not close: [`skill_drift.py` only checks one direction](../issues/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00CN89ERE8000) and [`norm()` runs before the `Supersedes:` strip](../issues/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00CNX13PMR001), the second of which bears on new delta entries carrying a `Supersedes:` line.

Every finding path (unrecorded additions, unaccounted drops, accounted-for supersessions) only prints, so the exit is always 0. The only nonzero exits are `sys.exit("<message>")` (exit 1, message on stderr) at `:53` (no `AperasKG/Apeiron`), `:64` (missing skill file) and `:214` (no snapshot or delta), plus argparse's exit 2 on a bad flag. The counts for an any-finding exit are already computed: `len(missing)` at `:230-233` on the added side and `len(unaccounted)` at `:249` on the dropped side. Callers relying on exit 0 are three text references and no executable caller: `skills/aperas-orchestrator/SKILL.md:150` and `skills/aperas/SKILL.md:133` and `:277` (`... && aperas check-links`, so a nonzero exit would skip `check-links`), and `skills/aperas-grapher/SKILL.md:157-159` (run bare and with each flag, no chaining). Making the exit nonzero turns the step-7 verification chain from always-passes into a real gate; today it also passes with a stale v4.2 Status line beside a v4.3 delta.
- **Finding — nothing outside the skill files reads the `Status:` lines or the checker**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVKY8V6R006' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (coder survey) Grep for `skill_drift` and `skill-drift` outside `AperasKG/artifacts/` finds only the skill text lines above and the script's own docstring. - **Finding — how the drift checker reads a skill delta**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVMGWF40001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (read from `skill_drift.py` by the orchestrator, to elaborate the rest of the Grapher skill item) An entry is a block whose text holds the new skill text in full; the checker looks for each skill unit as a substring of the concatenated recorded text, and the delta root's own text is commentary that is never compared. A replaced unit is named by a `Supersedes: [title](#id/BlockNode:…)` line in the entry, which the checker strips before comparing and reads for `#id/` ids; one entry may name several ids, and a block made only of `Supersedes:` lines removes a unit with no replacement. The version label is the first `vN.N` in the delta's title. Skill units of 40 characters or fewer are skipped, so they can be neither recorded nor checked; the Status guard covers the `Status:` lines separately. The order of work is: the coder edits the file, drift fails and lists the added and dropped units (truncated to 100 and 80 characters), the grapher matches each added unit to the dropped unit it replaces, records the delta and re-runs until it exits 0 with 0 Status, 0 added and 0 dropped. Entries in an unreleased delta are updated in place; entries in a released delta are superseded.

The grapher worked around it with a `---` child on the entry. A blank line before `---` should avoid it; not tested.

- **Finding — the 10-second timer does not persist thread writes**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVPCH5J8002' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (user: "That means the 10s flush has no effect on threads, doesn't it?") Confirmed by reading `service.ts` and `dehydrate.ts`. Thread-scoped `BlockNode`, `ArtifactNode` and `FolderNode` records are excluded from the content mirror that the 10-second `flushIfDirty` writes, and are written only by `flushStateIfDirty` into `.state/`. That runs on a 3-second timer but does nothing unless `stateDirty` is set, and `insert`, `update`, `remove` and `retype` set only `dirty`. So a thread write makes the 10-second timer rewrite a mirror that does not contain it, and nothing the 3-second timer does touches it, until a view operation (`unfold`, `fold`, `zoom`), the garbage-collection sweeps or shutdown sets `stateDirty`. Filed as [thread flush](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVNZXVR8001), with the fix of setting `stateDirty` on any write to a thread-scoped node.

- **Finding — every `remove`, `insert`, `update` and `retype` runs a whole-artifact link-integrity check before and after**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVPG6108001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (read from `service.ts`, not tested) The handlers call `checkArtifactLinkIntegrity(store, artifactId)` before the operation and again in `withLinkCheck` after it, over the whole artifact, so one `remove` of a task inside a 600-block thread file costs two full sweeps on top of the removal itself. The earlier verify-slowdown issue ([verify slowdown](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CJ0202MG001)) named the same kind of operation, `checkLinkIntegrity`'s corpus sweep, as the one that went from low hundreds of milliseconds fresh to 12–55 seconds late in a long process. That makes the sweep a candidate for the removal stall; a lead for the investigation, not a finding.
  
  - Promoted to [**A thread-task `aperas remove` can leave the service CPU-bound for many minutes, during which every command fails and a graceful stop does not complete**](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVNX6A3R000)
- **Finding — a `remove` of a main artifact sets only `dirty`, which is correct for it**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVPG6108002' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (user: "a `remove` of a main artifact also sets only `dirty`, doesn't it?") `remove` sets `dirty` and flushes with `--flush`, whatever the node, and the content mirror it feeds is the right one for a main artifact, so main removals persist within 10 seconds. Only thread-scoped nodes need the `.state/` mirror, which is why the thread-flush gap affects threads alone. One loose end: a removed main node can leave stale `unfolds` entries in the `.state/` TreeView mirror until the next reload sweep.

- **Finding — the thread-flush gap is a routing mismatch, not a timer-cadence one**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVPK8PA8000' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (user: "the gap is the behavior mismatch between the 3s flush to `.state` and the main 10s flush, isn't it?") Both timers work as designed and their cadences (3 s and 10 s) are not the defect. The mismatch is that a thread-scoped node is routed to the `.state/` mirror when the store is dehydrated (`THREAD_PARTITIONED_CLASSES`, `isThreadScopedId`), but the dirty flag is chosen without that partition: `insert`, `update`, `remove` and `retype` set `dirty`, which feeds the content flush that excludes thread nodes, and never `stateDirty`, which feeds the `.state/` flush that includes them. The fix keeps one rule in both places, setting `stateDirty` when a write touches a thread-scoped node. Possibly related, not checked: the `.state/` divergence check stamps only `STATE_CLASSES` (`TreeView`), so an external change to the thread `BlockNode` file there would not be noticed.
  
  - Promoted to [**A write to a thread node never marks the `.state/` mirror dirty, so it exists only in memory until a view change or a shutdown sweep, and a killed service loses it**](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVNZXVR8001)

That commit added the `zoom` op with `stateDirty = true` and one `dirty = true`, and did not touch the `insert`, `update`, `remove` and `retype` handlers, which still set only `dirty`.

- **Finding — the service's memory is a serious problem in two parts**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVQ2HDJ0001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (user: "Such a constant growth and the 5GB size is a serious thing.") First, the old service (pid 220722, up from 16:16) reached 4.74 GB at 19:20 and 5.76 GB at 19:42, a rise of roughly 40–50 MB a minute over the last hour, with two threads at 100% CPU, almost no disk writes, and a 2.1 GB V8 heap limit that its resident size is far above, so most of it sits outside the V8 heap. Second, a fresh service idles at 1.05–1.5 GB (median 1.34 GB, maximum 2.18 GB) over 379 samples and 63 minutes, while the whole graph on disk is 3.66 MB of JSON-LD, about 37,000 quads; that is roughly 350 times the data size at rest. The fresh one did not grow over that hour under light use and light load from the grapher's updates, so the 5 GB climb needs heavier work (the thread-task removals, and a long uptime) than the sampler has seen.
  
  - Promoted to [**The ApeironNgn service's resident memory climbs to about 5.8 GB over hours under heavy use, and a fresh service idles at about 1.3 GB for 3.66 MB of data**](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVQ4Z968001)
- **Open — what the memory is**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVQ2HDJ0002' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (orchestrator, none of it tested) The store is Oxigraph's WASM store, whose linear memory grows and never shrinks, and each reload builds a new store; a leak in reload or removal could keep old stores alive. The earlier verify-slowdown issue ([verify slowdown](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CJ0202MG001)) put the WASM footprint at 850 MB to 1 GB and ruled it out as the cause of slowdown, but not as a size problem. To tell the parts apart the service needs to report `process.memoryUsage()` (heap used, external, array buffers) and the store's own size, and to be started with `--heapsnapshot-signal=SIGUSR2` so a snapshot can be taken when it is large; the sampler cannot see inside the process.

- **Finding — the coder's code survey gives mechanisms for the spurious "not running" and the removal stall**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVQFC3SG001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (orchestrator, from the coder's Turn 1 Report in `.threads/coder.md`, a thread node and so not linked; code-derived points tagged read, numbers tagged measured in a scratch process) Every request, `ping` included, goes through the single `enqueue` chain and `handle` has no `await`, while the client's ping gives up after 300 ms, so any operation over about 0.3 s, or two or three queued, makes the next command say "No ApeironNgn service running" with nothing stalled (read; the orchestrator checked `PING_TIMEOUT_MS`, `handle`'s `ping` case and the `enqueue` call). This is a mechanism for [the spurious "not running"](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVMPABY8001). Each `remove`, `insert`, `update` and `retype` re-parses every live block of the artifact with remark before and after the operation, about 1.7 to 2.5 ms a block (measured), so about 1.3 to 1.9 s each time on a 767-block thread file. A removal tombstones every embedded `Link` and `StringProp`, and each calls `removeDanglingUnfolds`, which scans every quad in the store, about 140 ms at 39.6k quads (measured); the cost therefore follows the number of embedded nodes under the removed task, not the block count, which fits [the recorded removal stall](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVNX6A3R000) pattern of 39 and 50 blocks fast and 42 and 31 slow. The 5.4 and 12 minute stalls would need about 2,300 and 5,000 such scans; whether those tasks held that many embedded nodes is not known, and the coder's run of an in-memory removal did not finish in 100 seconds, consistent but not attributed.
  
  - Promoted to [**A command can fail with "No ApeironNgn service running" while the service is up, and an unchanged retry works**](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVMPABY8001) (the queue mechanism)
  - Promoted to [**A thread-task `aperas remove` can leave the service CPU-bound for many minutes, during which every command fails and a graceful stop does not complete**](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVNX6A3R000) (the embedded-node scan mechanism)
  - Promoted to [**Every `remove`, `insert`, `update` and `retype` re-parses the whole artifact with remark before and after the operation, about 1.7 to 2.5 ms a block, so a write to a large thread file costs seconds before its own work**](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVQHBP0R001)
- **Finding — boot and shutdown cost grows with the tombstones, and sit close to the client's timeouts**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVQFC3SR000' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (orchestrator, from the same Report) Boot is all synchronous before the socket exists: rehydrate about 1.06 s, `tombstoneVacuousContainers` about 1.2 s and `pruneUnreachableTombstones` about 2.3 s even with nothing to prune (measured), against a client `waitForReady` of 5 s. The next reload, startup or shutdown prunes each tombstoned block with the same per-node scan, so every removal also adds roughly 140 ms per node to later starts and stops. SIGTERM runs in JavaScript, so it cannot fire mid-operation, and shutdown re-runs the sweeps (about 3.5 s idle) while `stopIfRunning` waits only 10 s, which fits "didn't stop within 10s". `unfold`, `fold` and `zoom` set both dirty flags, so each costs a full content dehydrate and a state dehydrate within seconds.
  
  - Promoted to [**Boot and shutdown cost grows with the tombstones and sits close to the client's 5 s ready wait and 10 s stop wait**](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVQHCEW8001)

- **Finding — measured: a removal's cost is garbage-collection time driven by external memory, not the scan count alone**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVQY28QR001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (orchestrator, from the coder's Turn 2 Report in `.threads/coder.md`, a thread node and so not linked; seven bounded runs on `/tmp` copies of the store, nothing written to the real graph or the live service) Removing one `#### Turn` (34 embedded nodes) cost about 0.6 s in the pre-sweep, 9 to 10.6 s in `runRemove`, 19 to 29 s in the content flush and 0.2 s in the post-sweep, so 30 to 40 s with the loop blocked, and the state flush adds 16 to 20 s. `runRemove` did exactly 34 full-store scans, one per embedded node, at 208 to 352 ms each. The heaviest task (122 embedded nodes) was still inside `runRemove` when the 60-second limit hit, after 60 scans, and the average cost per scan rose from 130 ms to 3,013 ms across them. Under `--trace-gc`, Mark-Compact time per ten scans rose from 1.0 s to 28.3 s of that window's 29.2 s, triggered by external memory pressure: each scan retains about 9 MB of heap and 21 MB of external memory until the event loop turns, and resident size reached 2.0 GB after 60 scans. Repeated scans alone slow down; 160 deletions did not, and a fresh `Store` did not restore the speed. Content and state flushes cost 3 to 4 times as much after a removal. A task of about 120 embedded nodes therefore plausibly takes minutes, which fits [the recorded removal stall](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVNX6A3R000) of 5.4 and 12 minutes, and the same retained external memory fits [the memory growth](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVQ4Z968001); neither is proven, because no run finished a removal of that size and `.threads/grapher.md` was not measured. The finalizer explanation for the retained memory is a reading of the numbers, since the Oxigraph source was not read.
  
  - Promoted to [**A thread-task `aperas remove` can leave the service CPU-bound for many minutes, during which every command fails and a graceful stop does not complete**](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVNX6A3R000) (the removal figures, copied into the issue)
  - Promoted to [**The ApeironNgn service's resident memory climbs to about 5.8 GB over hours under heavy use, and a fresh service idles at about 1.3 GB for 3.66 MB of data**](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00CVQ4Z968001) (the retained external memory per scan)

- **Finding — a subagent can message the orchestrator mid-flight, and both directions deliver at tool-call boundaries**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CVRB63Z0000' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> (user: "Now we do some small test to see if a subagent can message back mid-flight.") The orchestrator started a dummy `general-purpose` subagent on five 25-second sleeps and sent it a token message at 22:32:36. The message reached it at 22:32:50, as a queued command right after the tool call it was inside returned (it had moved its first sleep to a background command after the harness blocked the foreground `sleep 25`). Two seconds later the subagent called `SendMessage` with `to: "main"`; the tool answered that the message was queued for the main conversation's next turn. The reply reached the orchestrator at about 22:32:59, between two tool calls, while the subagent was still on its remaining steps and well before its final report. The round trip was about 23 seconds, nearly all of it waiting for tool-call boundaries on each side. `SendMessage` was a deferred tool for the subagent and had to be loaded with `ToolSearch`. The earlier survey found no subagent using it unprompted, and the `SubagentHandback` description says it is not a messaging channel, so the skills still treat the turn's end as the only reliable way for a subagent to ask. Origin and history (the user's reading: "it's clear why the one-shot handoff impression is strong: it was true until v2.1.77. Only very recently, was the SendMessage -- originally designed for Agent Teams -- retargeted to subagent!"): mid-flight messaging is the tool's first design, not an upgrade. `SendMessage` began as the inter-agent tool of Agent Teams, an experimental toolset behind `CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS`, where teammates run at the same time and message each other through per-agent mailbox files, delivered automatically (Claude Code docs, "Orchestrate teams of Claude Code sessions"; an early-February 2026 sighting of the toolset is from a search snippet only). In v2.1.77 (an issue of 2026-03-17 reports it) the Agent tool lost its `resume` parameter and `SendMessage` with the agent's id or name became how a finished subagent is continued, which is when it was retargeted to subagents, at first still gated behind the Agent Teams flag; the docs now also say subagents that Claude named can message each other. In v2.1.224 (2026-08-07) it gained delivery between separate sessions, with `ListAgents`. What the orchestrator did not verify: that before v2.1.77 no running subagent could receive a message, which is the user's inference from the removal of `resume`, and the exact release that first shipped `SendMessage` in Agent Teams.

- **Question — what defines a "turn", and why does one op not wait for the last op's turn when all ops are synchronous?** (2026-10-10, user, while the Grapher restructures the issues; answered by the orchestrator, no dispatch): the answer, read by the orchestrator from `service.ts` (lines 215 to 220, `enqueue`, and 698 to 727, `handleConnection`) and not yet confirmed by the Coder:
  
  - **A turn is one pass of the Node event loop**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00D0X6PVC0002' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> it runs one task (a socket read, a timer, an `setImmediate`, a garbage-collector finalization callback), then drains the promise (microtask) queue, then picks the next task. Synchronous code of any length, however many calls deep, is inside one task. Finishing an op returns to its caller and is not a turn.
  - **`enqueue` serializes, and serializing is not turn-separating**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00D0X6PVC0003' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> `queue.then(fn, fn)` starts the next op as a microtask when the previous op's promise settles. Microtasks drain before the loop moves to the next task, so when ops are waiting in the queue, they run back to back with no turn between them. When the queue is idle, each request starts in the turn of its own socket read and the loop turns before the next request arrives. A backlog (the 300 ms `ping`, the timed flushes and every client's retries all go through `enqueue`) is therefore the case with no turns.
  - **Inside one op there is never a turn**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00D0X6PVC0004' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> a reload, the boot sweeps, or a removal of 34 embedded nodes is one synchronous run, so its garbage cannot be finalized until it ends. That is the 88 s against 8 s measurement.
  - **Untested**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00D0X6PVC0005' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> the Coder's runs used a 300 ms pause between phases. Whether a zero-delay `setImmediate` yield is enough, or the finalizer also needs a garbage collection that V8 schedules by itself, has not been measured.

- **Question — elaborate on "stop creating the wrappers at all"** (2026-10-10, user; answered by the orchestrator from `dehydrate.ts` line 49, `node.ts` lines 251 to 258, 2089, 2196 to 2210 and 2242, `folders.ts` line 21 and `artifacts.ts` line 200, read and not yet checked by the Coder): there are three shapes of full scan, each with a cheaper form. (1) "All ids of kind K" (`allIdsOfKind`, a `store.match` over every quad that reads only `q.subject`): ask the store for the kind's type quads alone, or keep a kind-to-ids index. (2) "Which views unfold this node" (`removeDanglingUnfolds`, which scans all quads to list the views and then matches each): one object-bound match, `store.match(null, unfolds, deletedIri, null)`. (3) Per-node field reads (`wrap`, `readField`, one match per field): one subject-bound match per node. Beyond scans, rehydrate adds quads one at a time, which the bare-engine run showed costs far more garbage than a bulk `store.load` (4.7 s of Mark-Compact at 100k quads against 0.29 s). Untested and to check first: that every node has a type quad matching the kind that `nodeKindFromId` derives from the id, so the result sets are identical on a copy of the real store; and the cost of each bound form against the full scan. Nothing is implemented; the user has not chosen a fix.
- **Correction — "stop creating the wrappers at all" overstated it; the wrappers cannot be avoided, only made proportional to what is asked for** (2026-10-10, orchestrator, after the user asked whether a bound match's results are not wrapped too, and how JavaScript could access WASM without wrapping): the user is right. A bound `store.match` returns `Quad` objects as well. Read in `node_modules/oxigraph/node.js` by the orchestrator: `Quad`, `NamedNode`, `BlankNode`, `Literal` and the rest are wasm-bindgen classes whose instance holds only an integer pointer into wasm memory (`__wrap(ptr)` creates an object with `__wbg_ptr = ptr` and registers it with a `FinalizationRegistry` that calls `wasm.__wbg_quad_free(ptr)`), and `store.match` returns an array of them; each has a `free()` method that releases the pointer at once. So the cost scales with the number of results, and a full scan makes 41.7k Quad objects (plus term objects) where a bound match makes only the few it matches. Ways to avoid wrappers for a given need: ask for fewer results (bound match), keep the answer on the JavaScript side (an index), or cross the boundary once with a string (`store.dump`, `store.load`), which carries no per-quad object. Releasing at once with `free()` is also available and untested.
- **Question — how can a JavaScript-side index reflect changes made on the wasm side, and is whole-store I/O for large operations or for any operation?** (2026-10-10, user, after accepting the bound match as the first step: "not to litter every time"; answered by the orchestrator from `node.ts` and `store.ts`, read and not yet checked by the Coder):
  
  - **The index needs no view of the wasm side, because nothing else writes to it**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00D0XVRHER002' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> the store is in-process and every mutation is a `store.add` or `store.delete` at 27 call sites, 22 in `node.ts` and 5 in `store.ts` (the rehydrate encoder); no `store.update`, `store.load` or `store.clear` is used. The index is kept in step by JavaScript at the same points. The risk is drift, not observation; guards: route the 27 sites through two helpers, rebuild the index at every rehydrate, and have the verify run compare the index with a full scan after each operation. The subject set changes only at creation (first quad) and at hard delete (`node.ts` line 237), because detaching a child deletes only its parent and sibling-index quads.
  - **Whole-store I/O is for large operations only**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00D0XVRHER003' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> rehydrate (boot and reload) adds 46,519 quads one by one in `encodeDoc`, then scans the whole store once more to find dangling references; a bulk `store.load` of an N-Quads string and a JavaScript-side set of referenced ids collected during encoding would avoid both. A single insert, update or remove touches a handful of quads and keeps using `add`, `delete` and bound matches. The flush is a separate question: the mirror is stable-id JSON-LD, so a bulk `store.dump` does not produce it directly.
  - **Order the orchestrator recommends**: <a name='id/BlockNode:00D0XVRHER004' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> bound match first (the user agreed); the bulk load and the dangling-reference set for rehydrate second; the index only if the measurements show the bound match still leaves too many wrappers.
- **Question — the index is kind to ids, so how is it used?** (2026-10-10, user, correcting the orchestrator's wording "subject set"; answered by the orchestrator, read and not yet checked by the Coder): the index is a `Map<kind, Set<id>>` attached to the store (for example a `WeakMap<Store, …>`), and it replaces only the body of `allIdsOfKind(store, kind)`, which returns a snapshot array of `index.get(kind)`; its callers (`node.ts` lines 253, 984, 2089, 2196, 2204 and 2242, `dehydrate.ts` lines 136, 161 and 168, `folders.ts`, `artifacts.ts`) do not change, and the snapshot keeps loops that delete while iterating safe, as the scan's array does today. It is built from `seenIds` at rehydrate and updated by the two write helpers. What it does not remove is the per-node cost after the ids are known: callers then `wrap` each id and read fields such as `tombstonedAt`, one `store.match` per field read, so `pruneUnreachableTombstones` still wraps every node; that is the next layer to measure.
- **Question — why can a wasm quad not have exactly one `Quad` object on the JavaScript side?** (2026-10-10, user, stating the ideal interface; answered by the orchestrator, partly from the binding read earlier and partly from the orchestrator's understanding of Oxigraph's storage, which was not verified this session): the reasons are that the store holds quads as encoded index entries and no quad object exists on the wasm side to be one-to-one with, so each `match` decodes a fresh Rust value and hands JavaScript a new pointer (two matches of the same stored quad return different pointers, and `__wrap(ptr)` makes a new object for each); that a JavaScript identity map would need the quad's content as its key, which is what the wrapper exists to carry, and would be a copy of the store if strong or need the same finalization if weak; and that the RDF/JS interface the binding follows gives quads value semantics (`equals`), not identity. The ideal is reachable one level up, in Aperas: one plain JavaScript record per node (not per quad), filled by a single subject-bound match with the quads freed at once, invalidated at the write helpers. That is the same machinery as the kind index and would make repeated field reads cross the boundary zero times.

- **Question — what is the difference between `free()` and `gc()`?** (2026-10-11, user; answered by the orchestrator from the binding read in `node_modules/oxigraph/node.js` and the Coder's measurements): `gc()` (the global `gc`, available with `--expose-gc`) forces V8 to collect the unreachable objects of the JavaScript heap now; for a wrapper that means the small JavaScript object holding the pointer is reclaimed and the cleanup callback registered for it is queued, and that callback frees the wasm side only when the event loop runs it later, so `gc()` without a turn frees nothing of the wasm memory. `free()` is a method of the wrapper that frees the wasm side at once and synchronously (`__destroy_into_raw` clears the pointer and unregisters the finalizer, then `wasm.__wbg_quad_free(ptr)` runs), with no collection and no turn; the object cannot be used afterwards. Neither shrinks the wasm linear memory, which only grows; both make the freed space reusable, `free()` immediately and `gc()` plus a turn later. A freed object used again, and a double `free()`, are not tested.
- **Question — can `free()` solve the issue to its root?** (2026-10-11, user; answered by the orchestrator, not yet tested end to end): it removes the link of the chain that turns wrappers into repeated full collections, and it is not yet shown to remove the problem. The chain as measured and read: the code makes very many wasm-bound wrappers (full scans, one match per field read, a quad object per added quad); the wasm side of each is freed only by a callback that needs a turn; the service and the old suite run in long synchronous bursts that never give one; external memory then grows and V8 starts a full collection each time it has grown by a step, which frees little. `free()` frees the wasm side at once, so it cuts the middle link without needing the turns, which the scan test supports (external memory flat after the first scan). What it does not do: it applies only where it is called, so every site that creates and drops wrappers must call it (the scans in `allIdsOfKind`, the matches in `wrap`, `readField` and `childrenOf`, the two scans in boot and flush, the per-quad `quad(...)` and `store.add` in rehydrate, the term read from each quad), and a missed site keeps leaking; it does not cut the CPU of creating the wrappers (109 ms a scan with both freed against 140 ms measured earlier), so fewer scans still help; the wasm memory it frees is reusable and never returned; a freed object used again is an error; and it is measured only on a scan micro-benchmark, one sample, not on boot, reload, flush or a suite. The 50 ms pause did not help step 3 or step 5g of the old suite, so part of the cost may have another source that `free()` does not address, which is untested. A safe way to apply it is a helper that reads the plain values out of a match and frees every object it made, used at the sites above, so that no raw wrapper escapes. The next step is a measurement in a scratch copy, before any production edit.
- **Question — free at the root, right after each match from the store?** (2026-10-11, user: "So, to be safe, we should `free` at the root right after each match from the store, shouldn't we?"; answered by the orchestrator, design not decided): yes, at one boundary and not at each call site. Counted by the orchestrator outside tests: 33 `store.match` call sites in six files (`node.ts` 23, `dehydrate.ts` 5, `threadScope.ts` 2, and one each in `vocab.ts`, `tree.ts`, `store.ts`), 27 `store.add` and `store.delete` sites, and 51 calls that build a term (`nodeIri`, `predIri`). The shape that follows from the user's point: one store-access module through which every read, delete and add goes, so that no raw wasm-bound object leaves it: reads return plain values (strings and term types) after freeing the quad and each term read from it; a `delete matching` does the match, the deletes and the frees inside, because a quad must be deleted before it is freed; the terms built for a query are made and freed inside the module, or cached when they are constants such as the predicate IRIs; a test fails if any file outside the module calls `store.match`, `store.add` or `store.delete` directly, so a missed site cannot exist. Points to check first, not yet checked: whether `match` and `add` accept plain RDF/JS term objects (`{termType, value}`) as arguments, which would remove the wrappers created for the arguments; what a freed quad does if it is used afterwards; and the cost of the extra calls on a scan (the Coder measured 109 ms a scan with quad and subject term freed). Not decided; not a go to edit the files named earlier.

**The user: does the survey confirm "technically triples, practically pairs"?** (2026-10-12, user). Orchestrator's answer from the census Report (`BlockNode:00D214DTAR007`; read, with the structure points checked against `shape.ts` and `dehydrate.ts` earlier): yes, with four qualifications. For: the predicate set is closed (27 predicates, each a shape field or `parent`/`__siblingIndex`, none outside them in the mirror or in production code); the fourth position is never used; every shape field is read with its predicate bound and its subject bound (S,P,*); reverse lookups bind the predicate and the object on eight predicates only (`parent`, `target`, `links`, `unfolds`, `profile`, `path`, `handle`, `name`); the forms (*,P,*), (*,*,O) and (S,*,O) never occur in production, so the predicate is a constant at every call site. Qualifications: (1) two access forms leave the predicate unbound: `nodeExists`, an (S,*,*) match at 18 call sites that only takes `.length`, and the full scans (*,*,*) behind `allSubjectIds` and `allObjectRefIds`; both are node-level questions (does a record exist, which ids exist) and become direct in a pairs engine; (2) the closure is a property of the data and of the callers, not enforced: `encodeDoc` and `mintEmbedded` write any key they are given as a predicate, and the tests use made-up predicates (`count`, `flag`) and a foreign-subject quad on scratch stores, so an engine that rejects unknown fields changes behaviour and some tests; (3) pairs are not all single-valued: `set` fields hold several objects in an order (newest first, decided), and the `embed` fields own their children; (4) containment is written twice in the mirror (the owner's `children` and the child's `parent`), so loading must accept a repeated pair. The conclusion is a statement for `design/core.md`: the store holds a closed vocabulary of fields, each with a fixed cardinality and storage kind, and the engine's job is those fields' lookups in both directions.

**The user is surprised that folders store their full path; had thought everything was unified to deep-path semantics** (2026-10-12, user). Orchestrator's check on the real mirror (`Apeiron/FolderNode.jsonld`, 16 folders; `ArtifactNode.jsonld`, 54 artifacts, one pass) and the code read earlier: a folder or an artifact stores its own segment as `title` (`design`, `linking.md`), its `parent`, and also the full `path` (`archive/design`, `design/linking.md`); the root folder stores `.`; of the 15 folders below the root, the 9 below `archive` or another subfolder have a path equal to the parent's path plus `/` plus the title, and the other 6 are the root's children, whose path is just their title, so every stored path equals the join of the titles along the parent chain. A block stores no path: `toPath` builds it from the nearest artifact's stored path plus the slugs of the titles above it. So the deep-path semantics are unified for resolving references (one grammar, `resolveDeepPath`), and for blocks in storage, but not for artifacts and folders, whose stored `path` is a redundant copy of what the parent chain already says; the copy serves as the key of the "node at this path" lookup and as the tie to the file on disk. Consequences for the design: dropping the stored path would make the lookup a walk down from the root by title, which is the resolver's own walk, and would make "a path names one live node" the same statement as "live siblings under one parent have distinct titles", moving the tombstone question to whether a removed node stays among its folder's children (not checked); keeping it leaves a second copy to rewrite for every descendant when a folder is renamed (not checked how rename is handled). Both go to `design/core.md` as an open point; nothing is changed.

Orchestrator's proposal for the index, for discussion, nothing built (figures from the Coder's survey, `BlockNode:00D20GSWJG00F`, and the census, `BlockNode:00D214DTAR007`): (1) forward, per subject: all the pairs of one subject in one small list (a subject has 4 on average and 73 at most), answering "the objects of field F of subject S" by a scan of that list and "all fields of S" (the flush, `wrap`) by reading it whole; (2) reverse, per field: object to subjects, a plain list that becomes a set past about 32 entries (the largest bucket is 5,462), built lazily the first time a field is asked in reverse and kept up to date afterwards, so the engine supports reversal for every field without storing eight or twenty-seven of them up front; keys keep their JS type, so the string "1" and the number 1 stay different; (3) per kind, a set of ids, which answers `allIdsOfKind` (16 callers, each a full scan today) and existence; (4) writes: a field is cleared and rewritten (as `writeField` does today), a repeated add is ignored (containment is written twice in the mirror), and the reverse buckets of the old objects are updated; (5) no ordering promised, ids as the tie-break. Memory, from the Coder's prototypes of a triple-shaped store on 60,000 quads: flat lists cost about 149 bytes per quad (8.5 MB), nested maps and sets about 663 bytes (37.9 MB), so small lists, not a map and a set per subject and field. Open: eager or lazy reverse; whether a node exists by being in a registry or by having at least one pair (today: at least one); whether the engine enforces the cardinality and the closed vocabulary from the shapes or the layer above does; the choice between one list per subject (record) and one table per field, which the user postponed and which does not change the interface.

Orchestrator's account, all from the Coder's survey entry for option (a) (`BlockNode:00D20GSWJG00F`) and the census, repeated without re-measuring: "4 on average and 73 at most" is the number of pairs per subject on the real data (mean 4.0, maximum 73), measured by the Coder on a copy of the mirror; "5,462" is the size of the largest reverse bucket on the same data (the bucket's key was not recorded in the entry); "27" is the number of predicates in the store in the census (the orchestrator's own count of the field names in `shape.ts` gave 26, not reproduced exactly); "149 and 663 bytes per quad" are the Coder's measurements of its two scratch prototypes. Mistake and proposal: the numbers are evidence about today's data and belong in the survey, not in the design; `design/core.md` should state rules (the forward pairs of a subject in one small list, because a subject has few; a reverse bucket in a set, because a bucket can hold thousands) and not carry the figures; the 32 threshold is dropped from the proposal (a reverse bucket is always a set, a forward list always a list), unless a measurement shows it is needed.

**The user asks what the largest reverse bucket (the "5k") is** (2026-10-12, user). Orchestrator's check on the real mirror files (`Apeiron/` and `.state/`, a quick script that counts, for each field and object, the subjects pointing at it; it counted 71,727 pairs against the Coder's 60,810 quads, so it does not reproduce the Coder's figure exactly: different moment, and the script does not merge repeats): the largest bucket is `type` = `listItem`, 5,881 subjects (the Coder's 5,462 is the same kind of bucket at its moment): every list-item block, most of them the bullets of the threads. Next: `key` = `position` (2,605 props), `predicate` = `[[wikilink]]` (2,600 links), `__siblingIndex` = 0 (1,826, every first child), `key` = `orderedList` and `startIndex` (1,556 each), `value` = `1` and `false` (about 1,550 each). All the big buckets belong to fields with few distinct values (a type, a key, a flag, an index) and none of them is among the eight fields the census found read in reverse (`parent`, `target`, `links`, `unfolds`, `profile`, `path`, `handle`, `name`). Consequence for the design: an eager reverse for every field would build and maintain thousands-strong buckets that nobody queries; a reverse built the first time a field is asked in reverse (lazy) never creates them. This supports the lazy choice; it is evidence, and the decision is the user's.

**The user asks whether the 5.4k bucket is only theoretical** (2026-10-12, user, on [the bucket check](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D23XPKTG001)). It was real in the Coder's prototype, which kept an object-first index for every predicate (the entry says the largest bucket "is 5462, so a set matters for deletes"), and Oxigraph keeps the same kind of entry in its own predicate-object index; in the design with a reverse built on first use it would not exist unless someone asked for all blocks of type `listItem` in reverse, which no production code does.

**The user asks whether a bucket that large can be real for `allIdsOfKind`** (2026-10-12, user). Orchestrator's answer: yes, and it is the one large structure the design wants. A node's kind is not a stored pair; it is read from the prefix of its id (`nodeKindFromId`), so the per-kind set of ids (proposal point 3, [the index proposal](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D23JGNSR001)) is maintained when a node is created or removed, not derived from a field. The `BlockNode` set holds every block: `aperas check-links` scans about 7,400 live blocks (7,381 at the last run), more with the tombstoned ones; the `ArtifactNode`, `FolderNode`, `TreeView` sets are small (54, 16, 17 in the mirror). It replaces the 16 full scans that `allIdsOfKind` callers make today. It is a different thing from the `type = listItem` bucket: that one is a value of a stored field, queried by nobody; `allIdsOfKind` asks by kind (`BlockNode`, `ArtifactNode`, ...) and never by block type. Promoted to [For each kind, a set of ids](../design/core.md#id/BlockNode:00D24N87SR018).

**The user asks why `allIdsOfKind` exists when each kind is already stored in its own JSON-LD file** (2026-10-12, user, asking whether it is because Oxigraph has no notion of that separation). Orchestrator's answer: yes. The files separate the kinds on disk (`ArtifactNode.jsonld`, `FolderNode.jsonld`, `BlockNode.jsonld`, `Profile.jsonld`, and under `.state/` `TreeView.jsonld` plus the thread-scoped blocks, artifacts and folders); at start `rehydrateStore` reads every file into one store of quads, and `encodeDoc` skips the `@type` of each document (read in `store.ts:70-111`), so the store holds no trace of which file or kind a node came from; the kind survives only in the prefix of the id. `allIdsOfKind` rebuilds the lists by passing over all quads and filtering the subjects by that prefix, and `dehydrate` needs those lists to write the files back (8 passes per flush pair, from the census). Two points: `rehydrate` knows each document's file and kind at the moment it reads it (it already keeps the set of ids it has seen), so the per-kind sets can be filled for free at load and kept up to date by creation and removal; and the files are not strictly one per kind, since the blocks, artifacts and folders under `.threads/` are written to `.state/`, so the write-back is by kind and by scope (the thread-scope test of the path), which the engine need not know if the layer above splits them.

**The user, reading `design/core.md`, asks for an example of "reverse, for each field, built on first use"** (2026-10-13, user). Orchestrator's example, given in chat and offered for the design's "The index": `aperas backlinks <block>` asks the engine which subjects have `target` equal to that block; the field `target` has no reverse yet, so the engine passes once over the pairs of the store, builds the map from each target to the links that point at it, keeps it and answers; the next `backlinks` call, for any block, is a lookup; a link created or removed afterwards updates both views of its pair, because the reverse of `target` now exists; a field nobody asks in reverse (`type`) never gets one; the reverse is derived, never written to the mirror, and is gone at restart and rebuilt by the next ask. Cost to state honestly: with the forward pairs held per subject, the first ask on each field is one pass over all subjects' lists, not only over that field; with a table per field it would be a pass over that field's table only, which ties the example to the open point on layout.

**The user asks why a set is better than a list for a large reverse bucket** (2026-10-13, user, from the design: "a bucket is always a set, because a bucket can hold thousands of subjects"). Orchestrator's answer: membership, adding without a repeat and removing cost one step in a set and a pass over the bucket in a list (removing from a list also shifts everything after it); at thousands of entries, removing a task of a hundred or more blocks, or loading a file that states each containment twice, would make thousands of such passes; a set does not promise an order, which matches the unordered contract. The price: a set takes more memory per entry than a list slot, which is why a bucket of one to three entries (the usual case for `target` or `profile`) is cheaper as a list; the Coder's prototype kept a list until a size threshold and then switched, and the design dropped the threshold for simplicity ("always a set"); if memory shows to matter with many tiny buckets, it is reconsidered by measurement, not by the design.

**The user asks about multiplicity: forward supports it, so the reverse should keep it to be reciprocal; are there cases where it is unintentional?** (2026-10-13, user, on "adding without a repeat"). Orchestrator's answer, with a question back: "multiplicity" can mean two things. (1) Several objects for one subject, and so several subjects for one object: supported in both directions by the design (the forward list of a subject, the reverse bucket of an object); each forward pair appears exactly once as a reverse entry, which is the reciprocity. (2) The identical pair (same subject, field and object) occurring several times, a bag: not supported in either direction; the store is a set of pairs, as Oxigraph's is, and a repeated add is ignored; "adding without a repeat" meant only this. Where (2) occurs today: the mirror states each containment twice (the owner's `children` and the child's `parent`), which is redundancy to collapse, not a count (68,035 adds make 60,810 quads in the census); a block that cites one target twice in its text has one `Link` carrying two `position` props (the `shape.ts` comment calls this "a real multiset"), so the repeated occurrence is carried by two distinct embedded nodes, not by a repeated pair; no other repeated pair was found. Where it would be unintentional: none found; if a count per pair were wanted, the occurrences would stay distinct nodes as they are. The orchestrator asks the user which meaning was intended.

**The user: the `Link` is the subject, not the block; the set is useful only if the same link can be added twice by accident** (2026-10-13, user, answering [the question on multiplicity](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2NMRN48001)): the multiplicity meant is that a source block has several `Link` subjects that point at one target; "I cannot imagine how that accident can be". Orchestrator's check in the code: the user's reading is right: each `Link` is its own subject with a fresh id, so a block citing a target twice has two links, both reached from the block through `links` and both pointing at the target through `target` (the reverse of `target` holds both links; the reverse of `links` gives the block twice, once per link); an identical pair can only repeat if one subject receives the same field and object twice, and the write paths already guard that: `writeField` clears the field before adding, `appendOrderedChild` removes the child's old `parent` and index first, `unfold` returns when the id is already unfolded (`node.ts:1250-1252`), and new `Link` and `StringProp` nodes have fresh ids so their pairs are unique by construction; no accidental double add was found. The one real repeat is the mirror, which states each containment twice (the owner's `children` and the child's `parent`), so the idempotent add serves the load and is otherwise a cheap safety net; the fact-check's finding of a child with two `parent` pairs is a pair with two different objects, which a set does not prevent. Two ways, for the user to choose: (i) the engine's add ignores an identical pair (a documented contract, cheap), and the loader may feed both statements; (ii) the engine adds blindly and the caller guarantees uniqueness, and the loader reads each containment once (from the owner's `children`) and only checks the child's `parent` copy, which is also the open point on where a node's parent comes from. The orchestrator leans to (i): the engine stays tolerant of the mirror's redundancy at a small cost, and the redundancy of the mirror is a separate decision.

**The user asks whether the current core stores a JS `children` list in RAM** (2026-10-13, user). Orchestrator's answer, from `encodeDoc` (`store.ts`), `childrenOf` and `orderedChildIds` as read earlier: no. The store holds no forward `children` pair at all: each child carries a `parent` pair and a `__siblingIndex` pair, and `.children` is computed at every access (`childrenOf`, `node.ts:71`): the reverse lookup of `parent` for the container, each child's index read, a sort by index; a node's wrapper object holds only the store and the id, so no list is kept in memory between accesses; the lists that exist are transient (the parsed tree during an ingest, the arrays `dehydrate` builds for the file). The mirror file does hold `children` arrays, and loading turns them into the `parent` and index pairs. Implication for the engine, offered as an option and not a decision: the engine could hold containment as the ordered list in the container (the mirror's own form) and derive `parent` as its reverse; that would make the index implicit in the position, remove the density gap and the two-parent gap by construction, and need the reverse of `parent` always built (the flush and `toPath` climb it constantly), where the present form needs it for every `.children`.

**The user: `children` and `parent` are separate fields; feeding both repeats no pair, so no idempotent add; "parent is the reverse of children" is semantics only** (2026-10-13, user, answering [the choice between (i) and (ii)](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2NVRNJ8001) and [the children-list question](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2NYY1FR001)). Orchestrator's reading and consequences, for the user to confirm: the engine treats `children` and `parent` as two unrelated fields; the mirror's double statement of containment is then two different pairs in two fields (the container's `children`, the child's `parent`), never one pair twice, so the load needs no repeat to be ignored; the engine's add is blind and its contract is that a caller never adds an identical pair (no write path was found to do so); keeping the two fields in agreement is the job of the layer above, which today does it in the `children` setter and `appendOrderedChild`, and which a check can verify; this settles the open point "where a node's parent comes from" in the design (a pair of its own, as the code reads it today) and removes "a repeated add is ignored" from the design's index; the reverse bucket stays a set for the cost of removal and membership, a reason of speed and not of repeats. One follow-up the orchestrator asks the user, because it decides what the `children` field is: whether `children` is an ordered list (the position is the order, no `__siblingIndex`, which removes the density gap) or keeps the `__siblingIndex` pairs next to it.

Decisions, which amend the previous entry: (1) containment stays as today: each child holds a `parent` pair and a `__siblingIndex` pair, and a container's `children` is the backlinks of `parent`, ordered by the index; the engine has no `children` field of its own, and the arrays in the mirror are the file form only; (2) a reverse bucket is a set, for removal and membership; (3) adding a pair that is already present changes nothing, a property of the structure and not a promise callers rely on: in this form the load does meet it (the mirror states containment twice, so the `parent` pair of a child arrives twice), and the property absorbs it; the previous entry's option (ii), a blind add and a loader that reads each containment once, is dropped, and "where a node's parent comes from" keeps its answer of today (the child's `parent` pair is the stored fact). **The user asks for the pros of tables (one table per field) in the layout open point** (2026-10-13, user). Orchestrator's answer: pros of a table per field: (1) it is the pairs model itself, a field is a relation held as one unit with its forward map and, once asked, its reverse map; (2) a lookup of one field of one subject is a direct lookup in that field's table, and an absent field is one miss, which matters because most probes at a flush find nothing; (3) building the lazy reverse of a field passes over that field's table only, not over every subject; (4) cardinality, storage kind and any uniqueness are attributes of the relation and sit in one place, and a single-valued field can hold its object directly, without a list per subject; (5) whole-field operations (all pairs of a field, clearing a field, checking a field's invariants) are cheap. Cons, for balance: reading all fields of one node (the flush, `wrap`) probes every table, mostly misses, where a record per subject reads one list; removing a node visits every table. Neither effect is measured; both layouts sit behind the same interface, so the choice can wait for the design to settle and be made by a measurement on the real mirror.

**The user chooses a record per subject, for modularity: nodes partitioned into the main graph, the threads in `.state`, and many external graphs** (2026-10-13, user, answering [the pros of tables](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2PGSFCG001)): "I prefer record per subject for modularity. E.g.: the nodes should be partitioned into main graph vs threads in `.state`, and many external graphs." Orchestrator's reading, to be corrected by the user: (1) the layout is a record per subject (all the pairs of one subject held together), decided; the reverse stays lazy; (2) the engine holds several graphs, each node belonging to exactly one: the main graph, the threads graph (today's `.state` content, the nodes under `.threads/`), and further external graphs; the records of a graph live in that graph's own collection, so a graph can be loaded, written and dropped on its own; (3) consequences: the thread-scope test, which today climbs the parent chain of every block at each flush to read a path (the filed issue about the thread-scope test and the cost of a flush), becomes a lookup of which graph holds the id; the files per kind and scope of the mirror become files per graph and kind; (4) not decided and listed as Open points: references and reverse lookups that cross graphs (a thread cites main nodes; does the backlinks of a main node include the threads, or does the caller name the graphs to search?), whether an id is unique across graphs or within one, which graph a new node joins, what an external graph is (its source, whether it is read-only, when it is loaded and dropped), and how the mirror files map to graphs. The Grapher records this in the design, with the pending Open point on a file whose `parent` and `children` disagree, and files the tool gap that a move with `aperas insert --after` and no body waits on standard input.
