**The user proposes partitioning the reverse buckets into a tree of "ports" mirroring the forward tree of blocks** (2026-10-13, user, on modularity): the forward and backward directions are totally reciprocal; a block A links to a block B through its children A1, A2, A3 (the macro-link A to B is reified by A1 to B, A2 to B, A3 to B, and deeper descendants), and each smallest block can hold many `Link`s at various positions; in reverse, the crowd of backlinks to B should be partitioned into a similar backward tree of ports B1, B2, B3 mirroring the forward tree (A1, A2, A3), so that reverse buckets stay at bite size. Orchestrator's reading, for the user to confirm before any discussion of merit: the reverse of `target` for a block B is not one flat bucket of every `Link` that points at B but a tree of ports under B, whose shape follows the forward tree of the blocks that hold the links (a port per source block or per level of the source's ancestry); a backlink lands in the port that corresponds to its source's place in the forward tree; the aim is buckets of bounded size. Questions to the user: is a port a stored node or only an in-memory partition of the reverse index; is the partition keyed by the source's ancestry, so that "backlinks of B from within section A" is a lookup of one port; does the idea apply to `target` only or to every reverse. Data point, not an argument: on the real mirror (2,840 links to 1,264 targets, links under `links` fields of the content and the threads) the median target has 1 link, 24 targets have more than 10, and the largest reverse buckets of `target` hold 59, 42, 37, 36 and 34 links, each from a different source block (the biggest are the issue entries of the performance work); the very large buckets of the earlier check were values of low-variety fields (`type` and the like), not link targets. Nothing is changed in the design: this is a proposal under discussion.

**The user on ports: dense future linking, partition by any hierarchy chosen by the caller; asks whether a port should be a stored node** (2026-10-13, user, answering [the reading and questions on ports](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2Q1WA28001)): the current links are sparse (object links); the future dense linking of `concepts.md` will make huge buckets of meta-links ("type" is itself a node, a concept, that gathers links); the simplest port tree mirrors the source's geography at some levels, not all; in general it can be any hierarchy, the next candidate being the IS-A hierarchy of tags and supertags (against the HAS-A hierarchy of blocks); the semantics are defined by the caller and the engine only supports the capability of partitioning ports into a tree. The user asks what the orchestrator thinks about a port being a stored node. Orchestrator's view, offered as a proposal and not as a settled point: a port need not be a stored node. Reasons: the buckets are derived data and the mirror is the source of truth, so a stored port is a second fact that must be kept consistent with the links it groups; a port can be identified by nodes that already exist, as the pair (target, an ancestor in the chosen hierarchy): "the links to B whose source lies under A1" or "under the tag T"; both hierarchies are already data (the `parent` tree of blocks, the IS-A tree of tags), so no new node is needed; the engine's capability is then "build the reverse of a field partitioned along a hierarchy relation named by the caller (and to which levels)", and a grouping the user wants to keep and name (an inbox, a curated set) is an ordinary node the caller creates. Against, honestly: a derived port is not addressable and costs a rebuild after a restart, as every lazy reverse does; a stored port could be linked and shown. In the same lazy spirit the partition could be made only when a bucket needs it. Not decided: the user has not agreed to any of this.

**The user: "lazy" means when needed, not ephemeral; a partition, once a bucket has grown, should be kept across reloads** (2026-10-13, user, on [the view that a port is derived](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2Q908ER001) and "the partition could be made only when a bucket needs it"): "Yep, that's the point. But by 'lazy' I mean 'when needed', not necessarily ephemeral. When a bucket has grown enough, it usually won't shrink and the partition should be kept across reloads." Orchestrator's reading and options, for the user to choose: the earlier reading that a reverse and its partition are derived and rebuilt flat after a restart is withdrawn for partitions; the decision to partition a bucket is taken once, when it outgrows, and must survive a reload. Two things could persist: (1) the decision only, a small record that the reverse of field F for target B is partitioned along hierarchy H to level L, while the bucket contents are still derived from the links at load and arranged as recorded; (2) the ports themselves as stored nodes, with their links. The orchestrator's view, a proposal: (1), because it keeps the mirror as the source of truth for the facts and the buckets as derived data, and the record is small; it could live as ordinary pairs on the target node (visible in the mirror and in git) or in a derived side file; (2) makes ports facts to keep consistent with the links and grows the mirror. Open for the user: which of the two, where the record of (1) lives, and whether a partition is ever undone (the user expects buckets not to shrink, so probably only by hand).

**The user asks to elaborate "the decision only"** (2026-10-13, user, on [the two persistence options](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2QDJ3T8001)). Orchestrator's elaboration, an example and not a design: a block T (say the issue entry with 59 backlinks) gathers links; its reverse bucket for `target` is one flat set at first; when it has grown enough (a bound chosen by the caller or by a policy, not fixed here) the partition is made along a hierarchy relation named for it, for example the `parent` chain of the sources, to a given level, so that a port is the pair (T, an ancestor of the source) and a link goes to the port of its source's ancestor at that level; what is stored is only the decision, four values: the field (`target`), the object it concerns (T), the hierarchy relation (`parent`), the level; what is not stored is which link sits in which port, since that is computed from the links and the current hierarchy; at the next load the engine rebuilds the reverse for T from the links and arranges it as recorded, and a link added later goes straight to its port; if a source block moves, its port changes by itself, because ports are computed from the current chain, so no content goes stale; if the recorded hierarchy no longer exists, the bucket falls back to flat and nothing breaks; the record could live as ordinary pairs on T (new shape fields; visible in the mirror and in git; a write to T when its bucket grows, which is a problem if T belongs to a read-only or other graph) or in a derived side file under `.state/` (not in git, kept across reloads on the machine, lost on a fresh checkout and then re-made when the bucket needs it); the difference from storing the ports as nodes is that nothing but the four values is a fact. Open: who sets the bound, and where the record lives.

**The user's analogy: a stored port is a mailbox with the mail inside; a stored decision is only the shape of the port, fixed to receive whatever pairs fit it** (2026-10-13, user, on [the elaboration](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2QFZENG001)). Orchestrator: yes, with one refinement: in both cases the mail itself, the links, is already stored once as forward pairs on the sources; a stored port keeps a second copy of that mail in the box, which must be updated whenever a link is added, removed or its source moves; a stored decision keeps only the pigeonhole layout on the wall, and the mail is sorted into it from the forward pairs at each load and on each write, so a letter whose sender moved lands in its new pigeonhole by itself.

**The user: the industry does cache indexes for fast reload** (2026-10-13, user, on [the mailbox analogy](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2QM1YW8001)). Orchestrator: yes; databases keep their indexes on disk (B-trees in SQLite and PostgreSQL, Lucene's segments, Oxigraph's own persistent backend keeps its index orderings on disk) and in-memory stores write snapshots so they need not rebuild at start. The distinction that matters here is between a fact and a cache: a cached index is derived data written for speed, with a rule to detect that it is stale (a version or a hash of the source it was built from) and to rebuild it then; it is never the source of truth. So caching does not change the choice between storing the ports and storing the decision: the decision is the fact; the built buckets, ports included, can be cached beside the mirror (a side file under `.state/`, keyed by the hashes of the mirror files, which the service already computes to detect a changed file) and rebuilt when the hashes differ. The cost is a second thing to keep right (stale-cache bugs); the gain is the time of a rebuild, which is small at today's size (the Coder's scratch JS store rehydrated the whole mirror in a fraction of a second, one run) and may grow with dense linking. The orchestrator's view, a proposal: design the cache as an optional layer behind the same interface, and build it when a measured rebuild time asks for it.

**Settled by the user: the stored decision (the port's shape, not the mailbox) is kept as metadata in `.state`; next question: how the caller sets the source hierarchy that the ports mirror** (2026-10-13, user: "OK, nail down the stored decision (the port shape, not the mailbox) in a metadata in `.state`."). Settled, for the next design batch: when a reverse bucket is partitioned, only its shape (which field, which object, which hierarchy, which levels) is recorded, in a metadata file under `.state/` (not in the mirror and not in git); the contents of the ports are derived from the forward pairs at load and on each write. Orchestrator's options for the next question, a proposal for discussion: (A) the caller names a relation to climb from the source (`parent` for the HAS-A tree of blocks; a `broader`-like field for the IS-A tree of tags), and the levels to mirror, counted from the root of that hierarchy so that sources at different depths fall into the same ports (the artifact, then a top section, ...); (B) the caller registers a function from a source to its chain of port keys, the most general form, but a function is code and cannot be recorded as data, so the metadata would hold only its name and the code must exist at load; (C) a small declarative spec: where to start from the source (the source itself, or a field of it such as its tags), the relation to climb, and the levels. Two points the orchestrator raises: an IS-A hierarchy is usually not a tree (a tag can have several supertags), so a link would fall into several ports unless the spec chooses one path, which decides whether ports are a partition or overlapping groups; and the split can itself be lazy and recursive: a bucket splits at the first level, and a port that grows big splits at the next level, so the recorded shape is a tree of split decisions, which is the port tree. The orchestrator leans to (A) declared per field once by the layer above, with the per-bucket shape recorded when the split happens; not decided.

**The user picks (A) and asks whether the caller can set a port size (a cap on the number of pairs) and let the engine choose the levels by itself** (2026-10-13, user, answering [the hierarchy options](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2QVB430001)). Orchestrator: yes; it is the recursive lazy split: when a bucket holds more pairs than the cap, the engine splits it by the sources' ancestors at the next level of the named hierarchy, counted from its root; any resulting port still over the cap splits at the level below; so each branch goes as deep as its own crowd needs, and a lopsided bucket (most links from one artifact) splits deep on that side only. Conditions to settle, a proposal: (1) the cap is soft: pairs whose sources share the same deepest ancestor, or have no place in the hierarchy (a source with no `parent`, such as the seven parentless artifacts), cannot be told apart by it and stay together in one port even above the cap; for the reverse of `target` this ends at one link per source block, so the split always ends; (2) splits are sticky: a port that has been split stays split when it shrinks, which is what the user expects ("it usually won't shrink") and is why the shape must be stored; without stickiness the shape would be a plain function of the data and the cap and could be recomputed at load instead of stored; (3) on an IS-A hierarchy with several supertags the climb needs one chosen path, or ports become overlapping groups instead of a partition; (4) the cap is set per field by the caller (or one value for all). Not decided.

Promoted to [Ports](../design/core.md#id/BlockNode:00D2T5VG08001) (the caller sets a cap and names the hierarchy relation, the engine chooses the levels) and [Ports and captured port views](../design/core.md#id/BlockNode:00D2T6KMXR001). The sticky splits of condition (2) were not promoted: the later decision that nothing about ports is stored replaces them.

**The user: non-sticky splits need no stored decision; the root rationale of ports is top-down traversal of backlinks, to handle them in bulk within a scope** (2026-10-13, user, on [the cap conditions](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2QZ6FYG001)): "If the splits are not sticky, we don't have to store any decision. Back to the root rationale for such a partition: the caller needs a way to traverse the backlinks top-down so that it can handle them in bulk. E.g.: when dealing with an issue about linking performance, we need only to check blocks pointing to the 'performance' concept that are scoped to {issues,discussion}/linking.md." Orchestrator's reading, for the user to confirm: what the caller needs is a scoped reverse query (the backlinks of T whose sources lie under given subtrees) and a top-down walk of the backlinks grouped by the sources' place in the hierarchy; ports are one way to make that fast; the answer of the query does not depend on the shape of the ports, so the shape is an internal detail of the engine; if so, non-sticky splits (shape a function of the data and the cap, recomputed at load) are enough and nothing need be stored, which would replace the stored-shape decision settled earlier ([that decision](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2QVB430001)) and needs the user's agreement to change. The example walked through: the pairs whose object is the "performance" concept are the bucket; a link's place in the tree is its owner block's place (the owner is found through the reverse of `links`); the engine keeps only the pairs whose owner lies under `issues/linking.md` or `discussion/linking.md`; with ports keyed at the artifact level this is two port lookups; without ports it is a filter that climbs each source's ancestors. That climb is the same one the thread-scope test makes for every block at a flush, so a derived record of each node's place (its artifact and its chain of ancestors), kept by the engine, would serve the scoped query, the thread scope and the derivation of the path alike; an observation, not a proposal yet.

**The user is torn: ports should be stable within a task, not flicker mid-task, yet a dynamic partition following growth and shrink is attractive** (2026-10-13, user, on [the choice](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2R93ZB8001)). Orchestrator's two ways to have both, proposals: (1) separate what the caller sees from what the engine keeps: the caller asks for backlinks grouped or scoped by named places in the hierarchy (by artifact, by section, under these subtrees), which are stable for as long as the data is, and the engine's ports stay internal, dynamic and invisible, used only to answer fast; a split or merge then changes no answer and nothing flickers; (2) if the caller wants the engine's automatic grouping itself (the level chosen by the cap), make it dynamic with hysteresis: a port splits when it passes the cap and merges back only when it falls well below it, and the shape is recomputed at load; in practice it stays still within a task and needs no stored decision. The orchestrator leans to (1), which keeps the cap a matter of speed and the grouping a matter of meaning chosen by the caller. Not decided.

**The user asks whether option (1) means the engine does a secondary split and merge from its ports to the caller's view** (2026-10-13, user, on [the two options](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2RDF208001)). Orchestrator: yes, at query time and without storing a second structure: the caller names the level or the subtrees it wants (for example the backlinks of the "performance" concept grouped by artifact); because the ports follow the same hierarchy, every port boundary is a node of it, so the regrouping is only of two kinds: where the ports are finer than the asked level, the engine merges the child ports under that node; where a port is coarser (or the bucket was never split), the engine sorts that port's pairs on the fly by climbing each source to the asked level. The cap is what makes the second kind cheap: no port the engine has to sort holds more pairs than the cap, apart from the soft-cap residue of pairs the hierarchy cannot tell apart. So the cap bounds the work of a query, and the caller's grouping never depends on where the splits happen to be.

**Settled by the user: option (1), separation of concerns between the caller's view and the engine's ports; next: how to keep the partitioning relation free of overlap** (2026-10-13, user: "That SOC is a nice resolution! The remaining problem is how to constrain the partitioning relation to have no overlap (like the supertag issue you posed)."). Settled, for the next design batch: the caller asks for backlinks scoped or grouped by named places of a hierarchy, which are stable as long as the data is; the engine's ports are internal, split and merged dynamically by a cap on their size, never stored, and the engine regroups from its ports to the asked view at query time (merging finer ports, sorting a coarser port on the fly); the cap bounds the work of a query. This replaces the earlier stored-shape decision. Orchestrator's proposal on overlap, not decided: (a) a relation can serve as a partition hierarchy only if each node has at most one value in it (a field of cardinality `one` or `optional`) and it has no cycle, so the hierarchy is a forest and every pair falls into exactly one port; `parent` is such a relation by its shape; (b) the engine checks both when a caller names the relation (it refuses a many-valued field) and keeps them as invariants while the relation is in use (a write that would give a node a second value or close a cycle is refused), which settles, for these relations at least, the open point on whether the engine enforces cardinality; (c) for IS-A, where a tag may have several supertags, the data keeps the many-valued relation for meaning and adds a single-valued field naming one primary supertag, which is the tree used for partitioning; (d) a question over the whole DAG (everything under T by any path) stays possible as a query that walks it and removes repeats, not as a partition. Rejected alternatives: the engine choosing one path by itself (implicit and surprising), and overlapping ports (a pair counted in several groups, so merges count it twice).

**Settled by the user: points 1 to 3 of the no-overlap proposal; point 4 to be elaborated with an example** (2026-10-13, user, answering [the proposal](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2RJBE9G001): "1-3: clear, OK. 4: let's elaborate on it with example."). Settled, for the next design batch: a relation can serve as a partition hierarchy only if it is single-valued and acyclic; the engine checks both when the relation is named and refuses a write that would break them while it is in use; for IS-A the data keeps the many-valued relation for meaning and adds a single-valued primary-supertag field as the tree for partitioning. Orchestrator's example for point 4, offered for discussion: tags `quality`, `performance`, `user-experience`, `memory`, `latency`; primary supertags (the tree): `performance` and `user-experience` under `quality`, `memory` and `latency` under `performance`; one secondary supertag: `latency` is also under `user-experience`. A block B1 links to `memory`, a block B2 to `latency`, a block B3 to `user-experience`, and a block B4 to both `latency` and `user-experience`. Grouping by the partition, the backlinks under `quality` fall into the port of `performance` (B1, B2, B4 through `latency`) and the port of `user-experience` (B3, B4 through its own link); each pair is in one port, and `latency`'s links sit only under `performance`, its primary path. The question "everything under `user-experience` by any path" is answered as a query instead: the engine walks the many-valued IS-A downward from `user-experience` (its subtags by any supertag edge: `latency`), keeping a set of visited tags so that a cycle or a second path is walked once, collects the backlinks of each tag reached (B3 and B4 for `user-experience`, B2 and B4 for `latency`) and removes repeats (B4 once): B2, B3, B4. The partition alone would have given only B3 and B4 under `user-experience`. What the engine provides for this: the reverse of the IS-A relation, built on first use like any reverse, and a generic walk of a relation from a node with a visited set; the caller composes the walk and the backlink lookups, and each lookup is served by the ports.

Promoted to [A partition hierarchy](../design/core.md#id/BlockNode:00D2T5XBH0001) (points 1 to 3) and [Enforcement](../design/core.md#id/BlockNode:00D24N87T000M) (decided for a relation in use as a partition hierarchy). The example and the any-path walk of point 4 were not promoted.

**The user asks whether the engine trims `latency` to `performance` to make a tree before partitioning, and whether the any-path query uses the partition** (2026-10-13, user, on [the example](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2RMQ6J8001)). Orchestrator's answer and a correction of its own example: (1) the engine trims nothing: the tree is a separate single-valued field in the data (the primary supertag), chosen by whoever writes the tags; the many-valued IS-A stays whole; in the example the tree keeps `latency` under `performance` (its primary) and the partition simply does not look at `latency` under `user-experience` (its secondary). (2) The example mixed two different things, which is the orchestrator's mistake: it grouped the links to the tags under `quality`, which is a walk over the hierarchy of the targets, the same thing as point 4's query, and not a partition. A port partitions the backlinks of one target by where their sources sit in a hierarchy: for example the backlinks of the concept `performance`, split by the primary tag of each source block (`issue`, `decision`, `measurement` under their supertags), or by the source's place in the tree of blocks; a source's secondary tags play no part in its port. (3) The any-path query does not use the partition for its walk, which follows the many-valued IS-A over the tags; for each tag it reaches it reads that tag's backlinks, and those buckets may be partitioned by their sources; the ports serve the query only when it also has a scope on the sources (for example "under `user-experience` by any path, only in `issues/`"); without a scope it takes each bucket whole, the union of its ports.

**The user corrects the edge in the question: `latency` to `user-experience` is the one declared secondary from the start and excluded from the partition** (2026-10-13, user, on [the answer](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D2RV7GM0001)): "I stared at the edge to be kept and wrote it down instead of the other edge." Orchestrator: agreed, and nothing is trimmed: the secondary edge is marked as such in the data when it is written, and the partition reads only the primary field.

Promoted to [A partition hierarchy](../design/core.md#id/BlockNode:00D2T5XBH0001) (a secondary edge marked when it is written and ignored by the partition).

**The user: the design is elegant, but the hierarchical port system should not live in a flat table, should it?** (2026-10-13, user). Orchestrator: right; a flat map from an object to its set of subjects cannot hold ports. A sketch of the implementation, a proposal and not a decision: (1) the reverse of a field stays a map from each object to its bucket, but a bucket is a small tree: either a leaf (a set of subjects) or a split node that records the level it splits at, a map from the ancestor at that level to a child bucket, a residue leaf for pairs whose source has no ancestor at that level, and a count of the pairs beneath it (the count drives splitting and merging and answers "how many" without a walk); (2) to place a pair the engine needs the source's ancestor at a given level, which is fast with a derived record per node of its depth and its chain of ancestors (the same record that would serve the thread scope and the path), kept up to date when a node moves; (3) for links the source is the link's owner block, found through the reverse of `links`; (4) a leaf over the cap becomes a split node by grouping its subjects by the next level; a split node whose count falls well below the cap folds back into a leaf (the hysteresis of option (2) applied inside the engine); (5) the costly case is a move in the hierarchy: when a node changes parent, every pair whose source lies under it may change port, in every partitioned bucket where it appears, so a move costs the size of the moved subtree; moves are rare (reconcile, a move with `insert --after`), and an alternative is to mark the touched buckets for rebuild on next use; (6) the forward side stays flat (a record per subject); only the reverse buckets that grow become trees. Whether this level belongs in `design/core.md` or in a later implementation note is for the user.

Orchestrator's reading, for the user to confirm before anything is built on it: (1) the records are arranged in the containment tree, a node's record held under its container's, as the documents are in the mirror, and not in one flat table of all subjects; (2) the forward hierarchy is authored by hand (containment), the reverse hierarchy is made by the engine (split by the cap); (3) a node's record holds both sides: its outgoing pairs by field, and, once a field has been asked in reverse, its incoming pairs by field, as a leaf or as a split record of ports; so the bucket of T lives on T's record, reciprocal to the forward pairs living on the subject's record; point 6 of the sketch is withdrawn. Questions the orchestrator asks: (a) is there still a direct map from an id to its record, used to follow a link by id, beside the tree (an index of references, the data staying in the tree), or is every access a walk from a root; (b) when a subtree is dropped (the modularity reason), the incoming pairs held on its records go with it, but its outgoing pairs into nodes that stay must be removed from those nodes' reverse records: is that clean-up the engine's job.

The graph modularity is another long story, but in brief, the droppable graph should contain no incoming pairs from the remaining graph, and its outgoing pairs should be cleaned up by the engine."). Settled, for the next design batch: (1) records are arranged in the containment tree; a node's record holds its outgoing pairs by field and, once a field is asked in reverse, its incoming pairs as a leaf or a split record of ports, so a bucket lives on its object's record; the forward hierarchy is authored, the reverse hierarchy is made by the engine; (2) a master map from id to record sits beside the tree as an aid for direct access; (3) a graph can be dropped only if no pair from the remaining graph points into it, and on dropping it the engine removes its outgoing pairs from the reverse records of the nodes that remain; the rest of multi-graph modularity belongs to its own design. Orchestrator's rewording, not yet confirmed by the user: "The engine stores pairs. On a node n, each field has two sides: the forward side holds the pairs n → v, where n is the subject; the reverse side holds the pairs s → n, where n is the value. **The wasm boundary as an amplifier, and the algorithmic costs of a write** (2026-10-14, user and orchestrator): the user: the wasm boundary is not RDF but amplifies the mismatch of RDF with this workload; orchestrator: yes: the boundary charges per crossing (wrapper objects for a quad and its terms, decoding, freeing), the edge layout sets the number of crossings (one per property read), so the cost is the product and RDF inflates the second factor; a node layout behind the same boundary would cross once per node. The algorithms, from the Coder's profile ([the filed cost of a write](../issues/core.md#id/BlockNode:00D22Z1HJ8001); 3 fresh processes, 6 inserts per case, a copy of the mirror): a small local change recomputes everything: (1) the path-collision check rebuilds the slug path of every live block (about 7,400), climbing each to its artifact, for one inserted paragraph: about 170,000 lookups, 1.56 s, whatever the artifact; a new block can collide only with its siblings, so a local check would do; (2) two link sweeps of the target artifact around each write parse every block's text (0.83 s and 0.78 s on the big Freeflow document, milliseconds on a small one); only the written blocks changed; (3) the timed flush within 10 s of a write rewrites all four content files: four full scans, 1.4 s, synchronous; a write usually touches one file; (4) the thread-scope test at each flush climbs every block to its owner (14,368 path reads in one flush); (5) `allIdsOfKind` scans the whole store for each of its 16 callers. These costs grow with the corpus, not with the change; a faster engine makes each lookup cheaper but not fewer, so they need fixing in the code whatever the engine; all five are filed.

Promoted to [The wasm boundary](../history/core.md#id/BlockNode:00D39EQJY0002) and [The algorithms of a write](../history/core.md#id/BlockNode:00D39EQJY0003) in the history.

**The user on two of the algorithmic costs: the path check rebuilds shared ancestors; a flush could be a plain dump if the records in memory have the mirror's shape** (2026-10-14, user, on [the algorithms](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D38VNQX0001)): "path-collision check: why rebuilding the common ancestors while we're all sharing them!?"; "The flush: if we set the objects in mem the same as the mirror, a flush then will be just a dump, isn't it? Orchestrator: (1) yes: `toPath` climbs from each block on its own (read in `node.ts`), so the slug path of a shared ancestor is recomputed once for every block below it; building the paths top-down, each node's path from its parent's, would compute each once, and a new block can only collide with its siblings, so no full rebuild is needed at all. (2) Yes, with conditions: if a node's record in memory has the shape of its document in the mirror (the same fields in the shape's order, embedded `Link` and `StringProp` nested in their owner, as records already follow containment), a flush is a serialization of the records of each file in id order, with no reconstruction from pairs; what remains to do at dump: the documents sorted by id and set fields sorted as the format requires (or kept sorted), and the `children` arrays written out from the reverse of `parent`, ordered by sibling index, since `children` is derived; the threads, held as their own records, are dumped to `.state/` without the scope test. Orchestrator's question: is a record shaped as its mirror document the intent, and is the dump first and the partitioning later the order.

Containment is the opposite case: it is not reified, and its extra information (the order) lives on one side, in the container's list (in today's code as a literal sibling index on the child). Orchestrator's proposal for the question: the engine is in charge of them, since graphs are an engine feature and membership in a graph decides dropping it, the sweep and the caller's dump per graph; a collection needs fast membership and removal more than positions, so a set; a JavaScript `Set` keeps the order of insertion by the language's rules, so a collection filled at load from the file (whose documents are in id order) and given new nodes at its end keeps id order as long as new ids are larger than the old ones, which they are when one process issues them in increasing time (observed, not guaranteed: a clock set back, or nodes brought in from elsewhere, would break it); so at a dump the order is normally already right, and the caller's sort by id (decided) becomes a cheap check over an already sorted list rather than real work; the collection itself promises no order to its readers, so nothing depends on that natural order. **The user asks whether a collection, if it is a set, is keyed by id** (2026-10-14, user, on [the collection proposal](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D3EAQMK8001)). Orchestrator, a proposal: a set holds its members by identity, so the choice is what the members are: (a) the ids, so membership is by the id string, and every use of a member (the dump, the sweep) goes through the master map to reach its record; (b) the records themselves, so membership is by the record object, which corresponds one to one with its id through the master map, and iteration hands out records directly; a map from id to record per collection would repeat what the master map already holds. Leaning (b): the operations on a collection (add on create, remove on delete, iterate for a dump or a sweep) all start from or end at a record, and a test by id goes through the one master map first anyway. Not decided.

**The user asks the difference between a set of records and a list of records** (2026-10-14, user, on [the membership question](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D3ECQGPG001)). Orchestrator: both hold references to the same records and both iterate in insertion order in JavaScript; they differ in what they promise and what is cheap: a set holds each record at most once and has no positions, so adding a record already there does nothing and testing or removing a record takes one step; a list (an array) has positions, can hold a record twice unless checked, gives an item by position, can insert at a place and be sorted in place, but finding or removing a given record means a pass over it and a shift of what follows. A collection by kind and graph is used by adding on create, removing on delete and iterating whole, with no meaning in a position, so a set fits; a list fits where positions mean something, which is why `children` is an ordered list. A list takes less memory per entry, and sorting a set for the dump means copying it into a list first, which is cheap.

**Settled by the user: collections are sets; their natural order, from snowflake codes that keep increasing, reduces the work of the sort at a flush, in line with "closest to the mirror but not guaranteed"** (2026-10-14, user, on [set against list](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D3EDBV6G001)): the main reason for a set is removal; adding the same record twice is not a realistic case. Settled for the next batch: each collection (one per graph and kind) is a set kept by the engine; its iteration order is the order of insertion, which follows the increasing codes, so the caller's sort by id at a dump is normally cheap; nothing promises that order. The orchestrator takes the members to be the records themselves (its option (b)), the user having chosen a set without naming the members.

Orchestrator's restatement, for the user to confirm or correct: a field is a binary relation between subjects and objects; its forward form is the set of objects per subject and its reverse form is the set of subjects per object (the backlinks), the two being the same pairs seen from either end; `one` and `optional` are the same relation constrained to at most one object per subject, not a different kind of field; `orderedContainment` (`children`) is a relation whose forward set is ordered (stored as `parent` on the child plus its `__siblingIndex`); a literal object (a string, number or boolean) is an object like any other, so a reverse lookup on a literal (`path`, `handle`, `name`) is the same reverse form keyed by the value. The orchestrator's qualification (3) in [the confirmation](../discussion/aperas-skill.md#id/BlockNode:00D21QR118001), that pairs are not all single-valued, is withdrawn: many-valued is the general case of a pair, not an exception. What stays open for the design: which relations keep their reverse form stored (the census found reverse lookups on eight: `parent`, `target`, `links`, `unfolds`, `profile`, `path`, `handle`, `name`) and which have none because nothing asks for it; and whether the set is ordered (newest first, as decided) or unordered with the order imposed by its consumers (the order-sensitive reads are `links`, `props`, `unfolds` and the `position` comparison).

Hypotheses, none checked: (1) V8 runs parts of a collection on background threads (user CPU was about twice wall time), and the cleanup callback that frees the wasm side is posted only when a collection has finished, so a zero-delay yield returns before it and 50 ms of wall time lets it run; (2) V8 starts a full collection each time external (wasm) memory has grown by a fixed step since the last one, so while the cleanup has not run every further step of growth costs another full collection (150 to 290 ms at this heap), and a pause that lets the cleanup run lets the wasm space be reused, so the growth and the collections stop; (3) a timer lets the loop block in its wait for the first time, which an immediate never does. The orchestrator's view: the pause length is a tuning that depends on the machine and its load, so it is a workaround; the deterministic remedies are fewer wrappers (bound matches) and `free()` on the quads, which the scan test showed keeps external memory flat. A short experiment on the bare engine could separate the hypotheses and find the shortest pause that works: scans in a loop with a yield of each kind (`setImmediate`, `setTimeout` 0, 1, 5, 20 and 50 ms, a forced `gc()` then a yield), logging `process.memoryUsage().external` right after each yield. - **Question — what makes the event loop count as a "turn", an empty stack?** (2026-10-11, user; answered by the orchestrator from general knowledge of Node, not from this codebase): an empty call stack is necessary and not sufficient. When a task ends the stack is empty, but Node then drains the `process.nextTick` queue and the promise (microtask) queue to the end, including microtasks that enqueue more microtasks, and only when both are empty does the loop move on to the next task (a due timer, a ready socket, a `setImmediate`, a platform task such as a `FinalizationRegistry` cleanup). So a continuation scheduled as a microtask (an `await` on a resolved promise, a `.then`) gives a new stack but not a turn, and a chain that always has the next op queued as a microtask never lets the loop go round; a continuation scheduled as a task (`setImmediate`, `setTimeout`, an I/O callback) does. Garbage collection itself can happen inside synchronous code; it is the cleanup callback that frees the wasm side which needs the loop to reach it. Whether a zero-delay `setImmediate` is enough to run that cleanup in the same turn is the untested point recorded earlier.

# aperas

Status: **v0** — factored out of `kg-doc-ingest`, which used to carry all of this before there was a second workflow needing the same practices. Everything here came from real incidents across two migration passes (`documentation.md`, then a `cli.md` → `cli-packaging.md` → `packaging.md` doc set) and the `aperas` dispatcher/packaging work that followed. Expect this to keep growing.

> **Aperas-repo insiders**: `aperas` isn't published yet. Every command below (`aperas <verb> ...`) actually runs today as `npm run aperas -- <verb> ...` from `Aperas/monorepo/`. **Delete this note once `aperas` ships as a real installed binary** (see `AperasKG/artifacts/issues/packaging.md`'s Pending Tasks — the `bin` build).
```

### Editing discipline <a name='id/BlockNode:00CE95MVP8003' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

1. **Graph-first, always — never hand-edit a projected `.md` file.** Once an artifact is tracked, every change — a wikilink fix, new content, a rename, a retitle — goes through `aperas update`/`aperas insert`/`aperas project`, never a direct edit of the file on disk followed by re-ingesting. Hand-editing and reconciling back in is the *disk-first* direction `kg-doc-ingest` uses for a genuinely new, not-yet-tracked doc; reusing it on something already migrated is reaching for the wrong tool, not a style preference (confirmed live, caught by direct user callout: doing this once for a wikilink fix, then having to redo it through `aperas update` to actually fix the workflow).
   
   - Edit one existing block: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CE95MVP8005' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> `echo "<replacement markdown>" | aperas update <path>` (targeting the whole artifact reconciles its entire tree; targeting one block directly only touches that block).
   - Add new content: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CE95MVP8006' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> pipe markdown to `aperas insert <parent-path>`.
   - Then `aperas project <path> --flush` to bake the change back to disk.
2. **Target the smallest block that actually changed, not the whole document.** `aperas update`/`aperas insert` both work at any level — a single list item, a whole artifact. Pushing a large, already-accumulated document's *entire* content just to fix one sentence means hand-reconstructing every other block exactly (any tiny transcription slip silently tombstones+recreates that block, losing its id) — and never do this by copying an already-*projected* file's content, either: it has `<a name='id/BlockNode:...' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>` tags spliced in that are a projection artifact, not real content — piping them back in bakes them into the block's stored text as if they were prose. Look up the specific block's id (via `aperas tree --depth <n>` on that subtree, or a direct read of `AperasKG/Apeiron/BlockNode.jsonld` if you need its exact raw text — see item 8) and target *that*, however deep it is.
3. **Wikilink syntax.** The link resolver only recognizes a URL that is `[[code]]`, starts with `aperas://tree/` or `aperas://id/`, or contains a bare `#fragment`/`path#fragment`. A plain `../folder/file.md/Slug`-style reference (no `#`) renders fine as prose but is *not* a graph `Link` — `aperas backlinks` on it comes back empty. Use `[title](../folder/file.md#id/BlockNode:<ID>)`, reading the target's actual anchor id off its own already-projected file. Verify with `aperas backlinks BlockNode:<ID> --text` (query the specific target block, not the whole-document path) — and don't just trust an `aperas update`/`aperas insert` summary line's own reported link-resolution count either; a real backlink appearing is the actual proof.
4. **The bold-colon gotcha.** A list item's lead-in-term anchor placement requires the lead-in colon to sit *outside* any `**bold**` span — `**Term**:`, not `**Term:**`. A bold-wrapped colon is rejected by the lead-in detector, so anchor insertion falls through to the next plain-text colon it finds, which can splice an anchor into the middle of unrelated text (e.g. into a link's own title). Match the `**Term**:` convention already established in migrated docs.
5. **Renaming a tracked artifact.** `git mv old.md new.md`, then `aperas ingest <new-path> --track --flush` from the *same* concern set you're renaming — no need to fall back to a full, path-less sweep (that walks the *entire* `artifacts/` tree, `archive/` included, which can hit collisions in never-before-swept legacy content and has no reason to be involved in renaming one doc). Scoped rename detection matches by exact abstract-text equality against already-tracked ArtifactNodes whose recorded path vanished from disk — don't just trust the "N renamed" summary line; confirm the *identity* was actually preserved (same ids at the new path) before moving on. A file rename alone doesn't touch content: if the doc's own H1 needs retitling too, do that as its own `aperas update` targeting the H1 heading directly with `--text-only` (safe as long as it has no `.text`/`.props` of its own to lose — worth a quick check first, e.g. via a direct `BlockNode.jsonld` read). Fix any internal cross-reference paths the same way, one leaf block at a time.
6. **Renaming a set of cross-referencing docs: retitle before you rename the file.** Do every content fix first — H1 retitles, cross-reference paths — while the files are still at their old names, verify, *then* `git mv` + track each one. That order means every `aperas update`/`aperas insert` call in the content-fixing phase still resolves against paths that exist, and the file rename becomes a pure mechanical last step with nothing else riding on it.
7. **A `--after`/`--before` anchor must be a direct child of `<path>`, not a descendant two levels up.** `aperas insert <path> --after <anchor>` fails with "anchor is not a child of X" if `<path>` isn't the anchor's actual immediate parent — a heading's own text content and its nested list are two different levels (the list is the heading's child; the list *items* are the list's children, not the heading's). If unsure, check the real structure first (`aperas tree --depth <n>` on that subtree, or a direct `BlockNode.jsonld` read) rather than guessing which level to target.
8. **No raw single-node inspection command yet.** `aperas tree`/`aperas backlinks --text` only ever show a *rendered preview* (title + truncated, anchor-stripped abstract) — right for browsing, not for verifying a stored field is exactly what's about to be pushed back, or for reading a field they never show at all (`props`, `tombstonedAt`). Until `aperas show <ref>` exists (pending — see `issues/packaging.md`), fall back to a direct read of `AperasKG/Apeiron/BlockNode.jsonld`/`ArtifactNode.jsonld` (a small Python/node one-liner) for ground truth.

### Working practices <a name='id/BlockNode:00CE95MVP800F' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

9. **Track your own view.** `aperas profile create <handle> --name "<Display Name>"`, then `aperas profile create-view <name> --profile <handle>`. Use `aperas unfold <path> --view <name> --flush` to reveal nodes you're actively working on, `aperas tree --view <name>` to render that unfolded lens, and plain `aperas tree --depth <n>` (no `--view`) for a skeletal title-only view of the whole corpus.
10. **Restart to double-check disk state.** After a batch of mutations (especially tombstones), `aperas service restart` gracefully restarts the shared ApeironNgn service (flushes, then reloads fresh from the on-disk mirror) — the clean way to confirm what you think landed on disk actually did.
11. **Stage each verified step yourself.** After a step lands clean (a stable round-trip, a rename that checked out, a reconciliation with no unexpected removals), `git add` it immediately — in both the code repo and `AperasKG/` (the graph mirror + docs). That turns the git index into a running checkpoint: if a later step goes wrong, `git restore`/`git diff` against the index recovers cleanly, no guesswork. This is staging only, never committing — `git commit` stays the user's own call. Pass `--flush` on the mutating call you're about to stage, not just at the end of a sequence — the service's own flush timer can otherwise land *after* a `git add`, so the index catches stale content and needs re-staging once the timer fires.
12. **Write discussion before executing, not after.** Once a design/plan is settled — even just agreed in chat, even a "yes, do it" reply — write it into the relevant `discussion` (or `design`/`planning`) doc *before* starting the implementation, not as a wrap-up once it's done. This applies to any nontrivial multi-step change (a refactor, a rename spanning several files, a new mechanism), not just doc migration. The reason it matters more than it seems: the conversation context a plan lives in can be compacted or cut off at any point, and a plan that only ever existed as chat turns is gone the moment that happens, with no way to resume or hand the work off from what's on disk. Caught live once (a 3-way workspace split was authorized in chat with nothing written down yet) — don't let it recur. Treat the `discussion` doc as a scratchpad, not something to only write once fully resolved: freeflow raw investigation notes into it as you go (inventory findings, open questions, even a "not yet decided" list), not just the final settled conclusion — that's what actually protects the work if context is lost mid-investigation, not just mid-plan.
13. **A heading-target `update` with no `--text-only` reconciles children too — even an empty-bodied one.** Piping just a heading line (e.g. `## Pending Tasks`, no body) to clear a heading's own stale `.text` looks like a pure retitle, but without `--text-only` it still runs the generic reconcile: 0 piped children vs. N existing ones reconciles as *all* removed, tombstoning real content (a live item planted moments earlier, in the live incident that caught this). `--text-only` is what makes a heading-text-only edit safe (item 5 already relies on this for retitles) — it overwrites just `.text`/`.title` and skips reconciliation entirely, confirmed via a direct `BlockNode.jsonld` read showing children untouched. Recovered the live incident via `git restore` on the staged `Apeiron/*.jsonld` (per item 11, only possible because the prior step had actually been staged) followed by `aperas reload -- --discard` to make the service pick the restored disk state back up. **Adding a new item into an existing list — don't target the list node at all, and get the piped line exactly right.** `aperas insert <list-id>` (or `update <list-id>`) piping a bare `- item` line reliably creates a nested list-in-list instead of a sibling item: the piped top-level list node becomes one new child of the target list, not an unwrapped item inside it — hit repeatedly across independent attempts (inserting, updating a list node directly, and once more piping a line that *included* the item's own ordinal marker, e.g. `3. **Text**`, when targeting that ordered item directly — the leading `3.` alone is enough for the parser to read the piped content as a fresh list, not plain retitle text; pipe just the bare content, never the marker). Piping plain text with *no* bullet marker at all is its own distinct failure, not a safe alternative: it creates a wrongly-typed `paragraph` node instead of a `listItem`, breaking a contiguous run into two pieces (confirmed via the actual projected output: the new entry rendered with no bullet and no indentation, sitting as a stray paragraph between two list runs).
    
    **Prefer targeting the list's *parent heading* instead**, piping the heading line plus the full corrected list (every existing item, verbatim, plus the new one) to `aperas update <heading-id>` — Stage A's exact-key matching reuses every unchanged item's id (confirmed via a direct `BlockNode.jsonld` read: `N matched` for the untouched items, only the new one shows as `added`), so nothing is lost, and there's no nested-list wart to clean up afterward. **This only works if the piped content is genuinely complete** — piping the heading line plus *only* the new item (treating it as if it were an append) silently reconciles the existing items away as removed, exactly the same failure mode as this item's first paragraph, just via a heading that already has real list children instead of folded text. Hit live doing exactly that to a 4-link Dashboard list, expecting a one-line addition to leave the other three untouched; it didn't — `0 matched, 0 added, 5 removed` was the actual summary line, not the harmless one-line diff it looked like. There is no shortcut for "just append one item" via a heading-target `update`: either supply the whole reconstructed list, or use the create-and-promote dance below.
    
    If a nested list-in-list (or a stray wrong-typed paragraph) has already happened, recovery is the same two-step dance either way: promote the real item out with `aperas insert <item-id> --after <existing-direct-child-of-the-list>`, then `aperas remove` the now-empty wrapper (or the stray paragraph directly) — or just redo the operation via the parent-heading approach above with the *complete* list this time.
14. **Freeflow documents as an unbounded tree, not a flat list of headings.** Refines item 12: give a freeflow `discussion` doc a few dedicated top-level slots right after the Dashboard — `## Open Questions`, `## Settled`, `## Checkpoints` — for whatever's concern-shaped enough to want a fixed home. **Moving an item between slots is a real move, not remove-then-insert**: `aperas insert <existing-node-path-or-id> --after/--before <anchor>` with *no* stdin piped repositions that exact node — anchor's current parent becomes its new parent, "cross-parent moves work for free" per `kgInsert.ts`'s own module doc — preserving its id, any backlinks to it, and its place in history, instead of tombstoning the original and minting a fresh one for what's conceptually the same thought. Caught live getting this backwards: promoting two Freeflow findings into a fresh `## Checkpoints` heading via `aperas remove` + `aperas insert` (piping reworded text) left two needlessly tombstoned orphans behind for a same-session relocation that a plain move would have handled with zero churn — left as a lesson rather than redone, but don't repeat it. Reach for remove+insert only when the wording is genuinely changing enough that it's not really the same item any more (an Open Questions bullet resolving into a differently-worded Settled one, say) — even then, a move followed by a separate `--text-only` edit is worth considering first, since it keeps the id and only the text actually needs to change.
    
    The reason headings are wrong for this: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CE95MVPG008' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> a heading is the tool for a *fixed, predefined* structure — the Document Topology's whole premise is that each concern doc has a small, stable set of headings regardless of how much content piles up underneath them. Markdown headings are also capped at 6 levels in principle (only the first 3 are practically usable before the nesting gets awkward), and — this is the part that's easy to miss — a raw Markdown heading has no real nesting at all: `##` vs `###` is just a number on an otherwise flat line of text; Apeiron lifts that number into a real parent-child edge, but the *source syntax* itself is dead flat. A list, by contrast, nests natively and indefinitely through indentation, which is the only structure that can grow unboundedly without the skeleton growing with it, and the only one a `TreeView`'s `aperas fold`/`unfold` has a real subtree to act on. When the Freeflow list grows long enough to clutter the view, fold its older entries by nesting them one level deeper under a wrapper item, not by giving them their own headings. Not yet exercised past a handful of entries — the folding step is a described intent, not a verified mechanism.
15. **Discussion is where all meta-info is born — not a sink for what didn't fit elsewhere.** This isn't just a filing convention; it's `AperasKG/artifacts/archive/Aperas-design.md`'s own Apeiron/Peras distinction applied to the Document Topology itself. `discussion` is the Apeiron-equivalent concern: unbound, schema-free, the Talk/discourse facet where every comment, assertion, deliberation, and reasoning trace originates, formless, before anything is decided about where — or whether — it belongs elsewhere. `design`/`issues`/`planning`/`history` are Peras: typed, crystallized projections that specific *kinds* of content get promoted into, deliberately, once a dedicated home for that kind has actually been designed. Most things never need that promotion at all. So something turning up mid-task that isn't what the task is about (a bug in the ingest engine while migrating docs, say) isn't a filing problem demanding an immediate formal home — it's supposed to start in *this* task's own `discussion` doc and simply stay there (Checkpoints if it's logged-but-parked, Freeflow if it's still being chased) for as long as no dedicated home exists, which may be indefinitely. Confirmed wrong live, in exactly this shape: two ingest/parser bugs found while drafting an unrelated doc's Task Breakdown got filed straight into `issues/packaging.md`, on the assumption that a finding needs an immediate formal home somewhere — wrong twice over, since `packaging` wasn't even the right *eventual* concern (it covers CLI build/distribution, not graph-engine parsing/reconciliation, which is really `Aperas-apeironngn-design.md`'s domain and has no live concern doc yet), and since reaching for promotion at all skipped past the point of having a discussion sink in the first place. Reverted (`aperas remove` on the wrongly-added items, `--text-only` restoring the heading's prior placeholder text) and re-homed as a Checkpoints entry with no outgoing link. The test isn't "is there an existing doc this could plausibly belong to" — it's "has a dedicated home for this actually been designed yet," and until the answer is yes, discussion is exactly where it belongs, not a waypoint.
16. **A piped `echo "..."` silently drops nested double quotes — that's bash, not `aperas`.** Content containing its own `"literal quotes"` (a quoted phrase inside prose, say) loses them when piped via `echo "<content with "nested" quotes>" | aperas update ...` — bash's own quote parsing closes the outer string at the first inner `"` and re-opens after it, dropping both marks with no error from anything. Caught live re-reading a projected dry-run: `not merely "wherever convenient"` had silently become `not merely wherever convenient`. Write content with embedded double quotes to a file first (a `python3 -c "print(...)" > /tmp/....txt` one-liner handles the escaping correctly) and `cat` that file into the command instead of an inline `echo`.
17. **A reconcile summary line's counts aren't proof new content actually landed where you can see it.** Pushing several new items into an existing list can silently match one's content onto an *already-tombstoned* leftover node's id (a stale test-probe, an earlier removed item — whatever last occupied a matchable slot) without reviving it, so it stays invisible (tombstoned children are filtered at render time) even though the summary line reports it as matched/added with no error. Caught live: a Resolved-section push reported plausible counts, but the projected dry-run showed one fewer visible bullet than pushed. `aperas project <path> --dry-run` and actually counting what's visible is the only real check — not the mutating command's own summary. Recovery is a direct `BlockNode.jsonld` read to find which id silently absorbed the missing content, then clearing its `tombstonedAt` directly (no CLI verb for this yet).
18. **Work the graph, not a folder of files — dense linking, deep read, deep write, and an active view are the actual point, not optional polish.** `AperasKG/artifacts/archive/Aperas-design.md`'s own philosophy names this directly: *dense linking* (everything related gets linked, either directly — A references B — or indirectly, via a discussion that talks about both), *deep read* (examining a block means reading its linked blocks too, not just its sub-blocks, and checking backlinks once the search scope widens), and *deep write* (updating a block means checking its backlinks and forward links to update what's related, not leaving them stale). Skipping all three and just reading/writing one doc at a time — however carefully — is using Aperas like a folder of markdown files pulled out book by book, memory standing in for the graph's own crosslinks; the graph's whole advantage over that is structural, not something extra to layer on once the "real" work is done. Caught live, three ways in one sitting: (1) closed out a gap in `list-consumption.md` that directly resolved a gap filed in `treeview.md`, and a second gap sitting right next to it, without ever linking the two docs together — a real wikilink existed one hop away (the origin `discussion/archive-migration.md` entry both gaps trace back to) and was never followed or backfilled; (2) declared "no causal story" for a stale-looking bug without first checking `aperas backlinks` on it, which would have shown zero backlinks — itself evidence the report may never have been reproduced, not just unexplained; (3) a `--view <name>` created early in a session and never touched again silently goes stale — it still answers `aperas tree --view <name>`, just showing whatever was unfolded during a *previous* task, and nothing warns that it no longer reflects current work. Concretely: before answering "why"/"is this related to X" from memory, run `aperas backlinks <id> --text` and follow at least one hop of any link already on the block; before closing an issue a design/fix resolves, link the two directly (both directions, not just the direction that happened to get written first); and `aperas unfold <path> --view <name>` whatever you're actually working on *as* you start it, not as an afterthought — a view left pointing at last session's work is worse than no view, since it looks current without being current.

### Reference <a name='id/BlockNode:00CE95MVPG00D' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

- `AperasKG/artifacts/design/linking.md` is the canonical spec for the addressing/anchor/wikilink syntax referenced in items 3 and 4 — read it when a link isn't resolving and the reason isn't obvious.
- `AperasKG/artifacts/design/documentation.md` describes the concern taxonomy (design/issues/planning/history/discussion) these docs get sorted into, and the Freeflow-document pattern item 12 above is built on.

## v1 SKILL.md (verbatim, 2026-09-13) <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4Q8001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

Dumped verbatim from `skills/aperas/SKILL.md` (reached by symlink from `.agents/skills/` and `.claude/skills/`), the same way [v0](#id/BlockNode:00CE95MVP8001) was — a copy rather than a live projection, deliberately, so successive versions sit side by side and what a restructure *drops* stays findable. That is not hypothetical: v0's presence here is the only reason item 18's third trigger was found missing from v1. Frontmatter and top-matter are kept as one code block; section headings are demoted one level so every item below stays individually addressable.

```
---
name: aperas
description: Working directly with the Apeiron knowledge graph via the `aperas` CLI — the graph is the source and the `.md` files under `artifacts/` are projections of it, so every change goes through the CLI rather than a file edit. Covers traversal-first reading (deep read/deep write/dense linking), the edit loop, citation direction, staging, wikilink and anchor syntax, renaming, and the current tool gaps. Use this whenever work touches the AperasKG graph in any way — editing/updating/inserting/removing/renaming a node, adding a wikilink, or any mention of `aperas`/`kg:` commands in this project — even if the user doesn't name the skill. Read this before `kg-doc-ingest`, which covers getting existing text *into* the graph.

# aperas

Status: **v1** — restructured from a flat, incident-ordered list of eighteen items into four levels, abstract to concrete. Content is unchanged except where marked superseded; the arrangement was the defect. Concern docs: `AperasKG/artifacts/{design,issues,planning,history,discussion}/aperas-skill.md`.

> **Aperas-repo insiders**: `aperas` isn't published yet. Every command below (`aperas <verb> ...`) actually runs today as `npm run aperas -- <verb> ...` from `Aperas/monorepo/`. **Delete this note once `aperas` ships as a real installed binary** (see `AperasKG/artifacts/issues/packaging.md`'s Pending Tasks — the `bin` build).

### How to read this <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QG001' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

Four levels, each following from the one above:

1. **Philosophy** — what the graph *is*. Everything else is a consequence.
2. **Orientation** — what reading and writing *mean* here.
3. **Discipline** — how to behave once oriented.
4. **Mechanics** — how to type it.

Read top-down. Stopping after Orientation should already leave you acting correctly in the ordinary case; starting at Mechanics gives you a list of gotchas with nothing to hang them on. An item sits at the level that explains *why* it is true, not the level where it was first noticed.

Each item is marked **[current]**, **[superseded]** (the cause has since been removed — kept so the old advice isn't re-derived), or **[unverified]** (described, not yet confirmed live).

#### Scope <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QG008' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

This skill owns *working the graph*. `kg-doc-ingest` owns *getting existing text into it* — tracking, ingesting, round-trip verification. Anything that is a fact about this project rather than about the tooling belongs in a concern doc under `AperasKG/artifacts/`, which this skill only points at.

Note the boundary is by subject, not by timing: <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QG009' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> a genuinely new document needs no disk authoring at all (see *Sketching a structure*, Mechanics). What is ruled out is authoring a *finished* document on disk and reconciling it back in.

---

### 1. Philosophy <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QG00B' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

**The Apeiron is the source; the `.md` files under `artifacts/` are shadows it casts.** [current]

A projection can be regenerated from the graph at any time. It is never the place a change is made. Editing a projection to change the graph is mistaking the shadow for the thing casting it — and it can appear to work, because the file looks right afterwards, while the source is untouched or gets reconciled back into a shape nobody chose.

The graph's substance is nodes *and the links between them*. A node's meaning is not carried by its own text alone; it is constituted by what it links to, what links back, and where it sits among its siblings and its thread.

Every rule below is downstream of this. "Graph-first, always" is its first consequence, not an independent instruction.

**Worked example — the same task, both ways.** Asked whether two docs cross-referenced each other, one session reached for `grep` over the projected `.md` files plus a raw `BlockNode.jsonld` read. It took several steps, produced an answer, and still had to be redone — because the question was about link structure, which exists in the source and only *appears* in the shadow. Redone properly it was one command:

```bash
aperas backlinks BlockNode:00CE1GW638007 --text
# → "No backlinks found."
```

That is the whole answer, from the source, in one call. Searching projections for structure that only exists in the graph is the same category error as editing them — one level down.

---

### 2. Orientation <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QG00K' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

**Traversal is the primary mode of work, not a check appended to it.** [current] Reading means following links; writing means placing them.

`archive/Aperas-design.md`'s Multi-Agent Projection Pattern names these as the architecture's own capabilities. They are crystallized practice rather than theory — but the practice predates this system, coming from years of real knowledge-graph work in Logseq and carried in as design instead of being rediscovered here. That this system has barely exercised them yet is a fact about its infancy, not their standing.

#### Deep read runs in two directions <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QG00N' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

They answer different questions, and the tool surface already carves them apart:

- **Forward and downward — deeper *content*.** A block's children and its outgoing links: what it is made of and what it refers to. This is what an ordinary read wants, and it is why `aperas unfold <ref>` previews children *and* forward links together — both are content, in the same sense.
- **Backward — deeper *context*.** Who depends on this block, who cites it, what surrounds it. `aperas backlinks <id> --text` stands alone as a command because it is the other axis. Reach for it when the decision is harder than reading: editing, or an investigation whose scope has widened.

**Deep write is inherently backward.** [current] What a change breaks is only answerable from the citing side. Updating a block means checking its backlinks and forward links and updating what the change has made stale — not leaving them to rot.

**Dense linking is the precondition for both.** [current] Everything related gets linked, directly (A references B) or indirectly (a discussion node that talks about both). A sparsely linked graph gives deep read nothing to descend into and deep write nothing to follow. Linking is constitutive here, not tidiness.

**Keep an active view, and keep it current.** [current] Set one up once:

```bash
aperas profile create <handle> --name "<Display Name>"
aperas profile create-view <name> --profile <handle>
```

Then `aperas unfold <path> --view <name> --flush` whatever you are working on *as* you start it, `aperas tree --view <name>` to render that lens, `aperas fold` to collapse a subtree again, and plain `aperas tree --depth <n>` (no `--view`) for a skeletal title-only map of the whole corpus.

A view created early and never touched again still answers `aperas tree --view <name>`, showing whatever was unfolded during a previous task, with nothing warning you it is stale — worse than no view, because it looks current without being current.

**Worked example — a traversal, start to finish.**

```bash
aperas unfold BlockNode:00CE0HD0HG007 --view my-view --flush
# → the block's own text, plus each forward link previewed:
#   │ ...Link... [[wikilink]] → BlockNode:00CE1GW638002  ## Open Issues  [+6]
aperas unfold BlockNode:00CE1GW638002 --view my-view --flush
# → that heading's children, one of which is the block actually being looked for
```

Two commands, each one hop. The content axis, followed until it arrives.

---

### 3. Discipline <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QG012' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

#### The edit loop <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QG013' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

The shape of nearly every real task:

1. **Orient before touching anything — content first, context when the decision is hard.** Start with `aperas unfold <ref>` for children and forward links. Escalate to `aperas backlinks <id> --text` for context. Editing always qualifies, because step 5 cannot work without it.
2. **Locate the smallest block that actually changed.** [current] Not the artifact, not the enclosing heading: the leaf whose content is wrong. `aperas update`/`aperas insert` work at any level, and targeting something larger means hand-reconstructing every unchanged sibling exactly — where one transcription slip silently tombstones that block and mints a fresh id in its place. **Never reconstruct by copying from an already-*projected* file**: it has anchor tags spliced in that are a projection artifact, not content, and piping them back bakes them into the block's stored text as prose.
3. **Edit graph-first.** [current] Pipe replacement content to `aperas update <id>`; `aperas insert` for genuinely new content; a stdin-less `insert` to *move* a node rather than recreate it. Never a direct edit of the file on disk followed by re-ingesting — that is `kg-doc-ingest`'s disk-first direction, correct only for text not yet in the graph. (Caught live by direct user callout: doing this once for a wikilink fix, then having to redo it through `aperas update` to actually fix the workflow.)
4. **Verify by traversal, not by the summary line.** [current] A reconcile count reports what the command *believes* it did. Proof is a backlink that actually resolves, or `aperas project <path> --dry-run` where the content is actually visible. A push can silently match new content onto an already-tombstoned node's id without reviving it, so it stays invisible while the summary reports it as added — caught live when a Resolved section rendered one fewer bullet than was pushed.
5. **Deep write — follow what the change made stale.** Check backlinks and forward links; update what now disagrees.
6. **Project, then stage.** `aperas project <path> --flush`, then `git add` immediately.

#### Stage each verified step <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QR005' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

[current] After a step lands clean, `git add` it — in both the code repo and `AperasKG/`. The index becomes a running checkpoint: if a later step goes wrong, `git restore`/`git diff` against it recovers cleanly. **Staging only, never committing** — `git commit` stays the user's call. Pass `--flush` on the mutating call you are about to stage, not just at the end of a sequence; the service's own flush timer can otherwise land *after* a `git add`, leaving the index holding stale content.

This is not bookkeeping. Recovering a live incident that tombstoned real content was only possible because the prior step had actually been staged.

#### Write discussion before executing, not after <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QR007' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

[current] Once a plan is settled — even just agreed in chat, even a "yes, do it" — write it into the relevant `discussion` doc *before* starting, for any nontrivial multi-step change. The conversation a plan lives in can be compacted or cut off at any point, and a plan that only ever existed as chat turns is gone the moment that happens, with no way to resume or hand it off from what is on disk. Caught live once: a 3-way workspace split authorized in chat with nothing written down.

Treat the discussion doc as a scratchpad, not something to write only once resolved. Freeflow raw investigation notes into it as you go — inventory findings, open questions, a "not yet decided" list. That is what protects the work if context is lost mid-*investigation*, not just mid-plan.

#### Move a node; don't remove and recreate it <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QR009' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

[current] `aperas insert <node-id> --after/--before <anchor>` with **no stdin piped** repositions that exact node — the anchor's current parent becomes its new parent, cross-parent moves included. It preserves the id, every backlink to it, and its place in history.

Reach for remove+insert only when the wording is changing enough that it is genuinely not the same item any more — and even then, a move followed by a separate `--text-only` edit keeps the id while changing only what actually changed. Caught live getting this backwards: promoting two findings into a new section via `remove` + `insert` left two needlessly tombstoned orphans behind, for a relocation a plain move would have handled with zero churn.

#### Citation direction <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QR00B' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

[current] The concerns form an abstraction gradient — `design` most abstract, `discussion` least, `issues`/`planning`/`history` between. A citation may point **up** the gradient or **sideways** freely. It may not point **down**: a design block does not reference a discussion block, for the same reason a node carries a parent pointer rather than a list of children.

The one sanctioned exception is a designated index — a design doc's own `# Context` section, which exists precisely to index its concern's other facets, one link each. That is a single structurally-privileged reference, not citations scattered through the body.

#### Promotion links at the origin <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QR00D' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

[current] The rule above has a corollary that has to be acted on in the same breath as a promotion. When a finding crystallizes *up* out of `discussion` into `issues`/`design`/`planning`/`history`, the new entry cannot cite the discussion entry it came from — that is a down-citation. So the link is added at the **origin** instead: the discussion entry gains "promoted to `issues/<concern>.md`" with a real wikilink, pointing up. The provenance then surfaces from the new entry's side for free, as a backlink.

Do it at the moment of promotion, not as a later tidying pass. A formal doc whose entries paraphrase confirmed findings without linking them reads as complete from its own side — nothing about it looks unfinished — while `aperas backlinks` on every one of its entries returns nothing, and the provenance survives only in the head of whoever filed it. Caught live: seven issues compiled into a new concern doc from findings recorded across four different discussion docs, every origin left unlinked, noticed only by direct user callout.

This is the topology half of crystallization (`design/aperas-skill.md`): <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QR00F' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a> a relationship first mediated by a discussion node becomes a direct citation once it proves load-bearing. Link density is the product of that lifecycle, which is why `discussion` is where it gets paid for.

#### Discussion is where meta-info is born <a name='id/BlockNode:00CF46W4QR00G' class='aperas-anchor aperas-id'></a>

[current] Not a sink for what didn't fit elsewhere. `discussion` is the Apeiron-equivalent concern: unbound, schema-free, where every comment, assertion and reasoning trace originates before anything is decided about where — or whether — it belongs elsewhere. `design`/`issues`/`planning`/`history` are Peras: typed projections that specific *kinds* of content get promoted into, once a dedicated home for that kind has actually been designed. Most things never need promoting at all.

So something surfacing mid-task that isn't what the task is about — an engine bug found while migrating docs, say — starts in *this* task's discussion doc and stays there for as long as no dedicated home exists, possibly indefinitely. The test is not "is there an existing doc this could plausibly belong to" but "has a dedicated home for this actually been designed yet". Confirmed wrong live: two parser bugs were filed straight into `issues/packaging.md` on the assumption a finding needs an immediate formal home — wrong twice over, since packaging wasn't even the right eventual concern, and since reaching for promotion skipped the point of having a discussion sink at all.

See `design/documentation.md` for the concern taxonomy and the Freeflow document shape (an unbounded *list*, not a growing set of headings).
